text: In the first, second, and third chapters of Gary Paulson's "Hatchet" we are introduced to a thirteen year old boy named Brian Robeson. He is flying alone to go and see his father out in the Canadian wilderness. Brian has a hatchet that his mom had given him. He is very angry and confused about his parents divorce. While Brian is on the plane he is thinking about "the Secret". The awful thing he knows about his mom and another man. The pilot is very nice and is teaching Brian about how to use the radio and he even allows Brian to fly the plane for a little while. Then the pilot has a heart attack. He dies. Brian is trying to gain control of the airplane. He is so scared and panicky. Brian is trying to remember what the pilot was saying. He is trying to use the radio to get help. But no one is responding. He knows that he has to get this plane to land. He is looking for a place to land it. Then he takes the plane down towards the lake. He ends up crashing into the water.

The night before we played in the championship game for our school basketball team, I claimed I was prepared. But as soon as I entered the gym, I lost my nerve. The glaring lights were reflected off the gleaming court. The chants of the audience echoed like the roar of thunder. I dribbled the ball repeatedly but couldn't stop it from falling out of my sticky fingers.

Our coach gathered us together and said, "Just take a breath and prepare for the first play." I drew in a long breath, but my heart kept beating hard. As the referee signaled the game's start, I was stuck in place. Suddenly, I recalled practicing the first play over and over. So, I darted to my position and made the pass to Maya. She put it in the basket. The team went wild with excitement.

That's when I started to calm down. I even managed to swipe the ball near the end of the second quarter. We ended up winning by two points. What I learned from the experience was that being nervous didn't mean I wasn't ready. It was just a sign that I cared about the game. Now, if I ever get nervous about something, I try to breathe, think back to my practice, and make my first move.

That's become a practice that helps me channel my fear into energy. It also reminds me that being brave doesn't mean not being nervous. It's about going for it, despite having trembling knees.

Dear Editor,

Our school cafeteria should continue to have the salad bar. The fact that 140 students used the salad bar last week is evidence that it's not a waste of money but actually a popular and useful option.

To start, the salad bar allows for healthier lunch options. The fresh lettuce, carrots, tomatoes, cucumbers, beans, fruits etc. provide us with important vitamins and energy for our afternoon classes. It also allows for students to select what they want and the amount. This is especially good for those who have alternative diets or allergies.

Another reason the salad bar is good is the variety it provides. It can get monotonous to have the same hot meals over and over, but with the salad bar we can make a different meal everyday. Plus, it gives us the opportunity to try vegetables that we might not otherwise taste.

It may seem like it's a lot of money spent on the salad bar or like it's a waste. However, there's ways that the school can minimize waste by monitoring what's chosen and providing smaller containers. Also, with so many people taking advantage of the salad bar, if we took it away it may actually cause students to be less satisfied with school lunches.

The salad bar is great as it promotes healthy options and allows for students to make an important choice. I urge the leaders of our school to hear the cries of the 140 students who used the salad bar last week and continue to provide this beneficial option to everyone.

Sincerely,
[Your Name]

The conch in William Golding's Lord of the Flies is a significant symbol of civilization, order and the conch as a collective authority. The conch shell is used by Ralph and Piggy to summon all the boys when they first find it on the island. It becomes a tool of communication and a means of establishing order among the boys. The conch serves as an example of how essential rules are in society.

The boys establish that only the one who holds the conch should speak in meetings. This symbolizes democracy and respect for the views of others. At first the conch holds a lot of authority for Ralph, as he used it to be a fair leader and set up rules. The power of the conch is truly in the hands of the boys. They get to decide if it holds power or not. As their fear and longing for power increased, they begin to disregard the conch. The conch is not listened to as Jack interupts meetings. He refuses to abide by rules, and instills in the boys the need to focus on hunting and not rescue or cooperation.

The state of the conch also shows the decay of the civilization on the island. The conch is initially beautiful and serves a purpose. As the boys get more savage the conch fades and becomes broken. That the conch is shattered at the same time Piggy dies is very important. Piggy is the character of reason and smarts, while the conch is the society that is there to preserve these values. When Roger smashes the conch and Piggy, Golding is making the point that there is no order left or civility left.

The conch represents the delicate balance of civilization. It can set rules but not make people follow those rules. It takes the individual wanting to abide by laws, work together and follow rights of others in order for civilization to survive, as Golding implies.

Book Report on the Outsiders

The Outsiders by S.E. Hinton published in 1967 is a coming of age story that follows a fourteen year old boy named Ponyboy Curtis, a member of the Greasers. They are always in a fight with another group of kids called Socs, which are the rich kids from the other side of town. Ponyboy is a greaser, but he is different than the others in the group because he likes reading books and watching sunsets.

Ponyboy's good friend is Johnny Cade. He's scared and so wounded from the violence in his life unlike Ponyboy. After getting into a fight with the Socs, Johnny ends up killing Bob in self defense after Bob tried to attack Ponyboy. Now Johnny and Ponyboy are on the run. They take refuge in a deserted church.

They're hiding out when the church goes up in flames. Ponyboy and Johnny save a few kids that are trapped inside the church. They are now the heroes, but Johnny is badly wounded. He eventually dies in the hospital. Ponyboy is affected after Johnny's death. He realizes that all of this violence just causes more pain.

The quote 'stay gold' is taken from Robert Frost's poem 'Nothing gold can stay'. It is said to Ponyboy by Johnny. He's telling him to stay good, stay optimistic and stay himself even though the world can be so harsh. Gold is a metaphor. It's about innocence, beauty, goodness that usually fades away with age. What Johnny is saying is for Ponyboy to not lose his kindness.

I think the Outsiders is a strong book because the characters are real and the conflicts are relevant. It teaches that you shouldn't judge a book by it's cover. Greasers and Socs have their issues and fears and dreams. Ponyboy learns to have empathy with people which makes things better. Hinton's book is a sad one, yet it's inspiring.

Initially, when I was reading Robert Frost's "The Road Not Taken", I took it as a kind of 'huzzah individuality' type of poem. There's a man in a yellow wood and he has two paths in front of him to choose. It seems like a life-like image of decisions we all have to make. There's no way to go both ways. Therefore, it seems his choice is a permanent and important one. I started thinking about all the times in my life where I've wondered 'what if I made another choice' and what my life would be like then.

However, when I analyze the poem's specific details, things get a bit more complicated. The roads were "really about the same". Neither had been more traveled. And actually they're pretty. And both roads are full of leaves. That doesn't sound like he took 'the one less traveled by' at the end. Often times, people get confused about the end because they'll remember the self-assured message, but forget about the irony and ambiguity of the poem. Frost never really makes it clear one way or the other that one path is more brave, better, different.

The end is also left ambiguous by the mention of this 'sigh' in the future. Will it be a happy sigh? Sad sigh? Relief? Just the realization that humans love to turn their choices into narratives? The man is imagining himself in the future telling this story 'ages and ages hence'. So memory is a powerful thing, huh? Perhaps he's even trying to give this common decision some sort of heroic reason. He's telling himself he made a different choice. Which in the poem there wasn't a difference.

For me, the poem isn't so much a 'screw conformity' piece, but more about ambiguity and how we interpret ourselves. Sure, our decisions are important, but often we're the ones assigning meaning. I think the point of the poem is to make the reader realize that you really can't compare the life you took to the one you didn't take. So don't be so self-assured about the end like it's some kind of motivation slogan. Instead, I think the poem is meant to make you question how self-assured you are about your own decisions.

The Treaty of Versailles and World War II

The Treaty of Versailles was a treaty signed in 1919 following World War I. The Treaty of Versailles played a part in causing World War II due to the resentment, economic depression, and political unrest it caused in Germany. Though there were other causes of World War II, the harsh conditions of the treaty were part of what allowed Adolf Hitler and the Nazis to rise to power.

One of the most controversial aspects of the Treaty of Versailles was Article 231. This article is often referred to as the 'war guilt clause'. It said that Germany and its allies were responsible for the outbreak of World War I. The war guilt clause was a source of great resentment for the Germans. It made them feel like the whole of Germany was being unfairly blamed. Germany felt disgraced, as they felt that they had been unfairly made to accept blame for the war. This is because the causes of the war were much more complex. Germans began to lose faith in their democratic government, as this government had been responsible for agreeing to the treaty.

Another major aspect of the Treaty of Versailles was that Germany was made to pay massive war reparations to the victorious powers. This created huge economic burdens for Germany. Germany faced issues of debt, high unemployment, and hyperinflation. In 1923 the German government resorted to printing huge quantities of money. This led to a state of hyperinflation. People's savings were now almost worthless. Many people in Germany lost their financial security. Though there were many other factors at play in Germany's economic decline, the reparations were a big symbol of the unfairness of the treaty.

Germany was also stripped of territory, military power, and resources. Germany was restricted in size of army, and was not allowed an air force or submarines. They felt isolated and humiliated. Hitler made promises to the German people to defy the Treaty of Versailles, rebuild the military and restore German pride. These were promises that many in Germany would have loved to hear, particularly those who were angry about the Treaty of Versailles and wanted things to change.

So, yes, the Treaty of Versailles was partly responsible for setting the stage for World War II. The 'war guilt clause' and reparations created resentment and suffering. Other restrictions in the treaty led to the growth of German nationalism. However, other factors such as the rise of Hitler, the global Great Depression, and the lack of a decisive response from other countries were also key causes of the war.

Dagger Soliloquy act 2 scene 1 Macbeth by William Shakespeare reveals Macbeth's scared and increasingly savage thoughts. During act 2 scene 1 in Macbeth, we find ourselves with Macbeth on stage by himself. He asks himself the rhetorical question "Is this a dagger which I see before me?" He is unsure of what is real and what isn't because of his senses. Macbeth could be seeing the dagger which could be supernatural but it also could be in his head as his ambitious thoughts play tricks on him. Shakespeare's character of Macbeth has two sides to him. He is desperate to carry out the murder but at the same time he is disturbed by his actions.

The mention of the dagger creates an obsession in Macbeth. He attempts to grab the dagger and says "Come, let me clutch thee" But he realises it is just an image. There is a stark difference between what he is seeing and what he is able to touch. This highlights his mind. The dagger seems to be directing him. The dagger is a sign for the murder and how Macbeth is losing control. When he calls it a "fatal vision" the word fatal implies death but also implies fate. Macbeth believes that this weapon is taking him towards his fate. Macbeth has chosen to go down this path but he cannot escape it.

Shakespeare includes blood imagery, Macbeth envisions "gouts of blood" on the dagger even though it's not real. It foreshadows the murder of Duncan but shows how violent Macbeth's thoughts are and how they are tainted. The darkness and allusions to "night" and "witchcraft" creates a menacing tone. It seems that everything natural and supernatural is conspiring against him. But Macbeth realises that it is his own "heat-oppressed brain" that has imagined the vision.

In the end of the soliloquy, Macbeth's short, to the point comments like "I go, and it is done" are a reflection of how he is switching from hesitancy to determination. This soliloquy is a point where ambition is triumphing over conscience. Shakespeare makes the audience sympathise with Macbeth's fear but we are also shown how the power of imagination, temptation and the lack of control of ambition can lead a person to monstrous acts.

Causes of the American Revolution

The American Revolution started when people in the colonies felt they were being treated unfairly. When the French and Indian War ended in 1763, Britain was in a lot of debt. Parliament, the British government, tried to get money by taxing the colonies. Colonists felt Parliament did not have the right to tax them since they did not have any representatives. Colonists started to say, "No taxation without representation."

The Stamp Act of 1765 was one important act. This meant colonists had to pay for stamps on newspapers, legal documents, and licenses. Other printed materials had to be stamped as well. Colonists protested with speeches, boycotts, and sometimes violence. The colonists thought the act violated their rights as Englishmen. Even though Parliament repealed the act, it still claimed it had the right to tax the colonies.

Britain passed more taxes, including taxes on tea. Britain sent soldiers to help enforce the laws and keep order. Many colonists felt they were being controlled. In 1770, five colonists were killed by British soldiers during the Boston Massacre. The colonists had more anger towards Britain.

In 1773, Parliament granted the British East India Company some advantages for selling tea. This made colonists unhappy about the new tax and the power of the company. On December 16, 1773, a group of colonists boarded some ships in Boston. They dumped hundreds of chests of tea in the harbor. This was called the Boston Tea Party.

The Intolerable Acts, which were punishments given to Massachusetts, closed the Boston Harbor and reduced self-government in the colonies. The laws did not stop the protests. It brought the colonies together. As more distrust grew, the colonists organized a Continental Congress. The colonists even began a fight for independence in 1775.

Life in ancient Rome was very busy and social. Most people lived in crowded apartments called insulae. Wealthy people lived in bigger homes called domus. People got up early and went to the busy markets to buy bread, vegetables, fruits, or fish. Rich children learned to read, write, and math while poor kids often learned different skills at home. In 80 AD, the Colosseum opened. The Colosseum was a huge arena where people could see gladiators fight, amazing animal hunts, and exciting shows. The people would cheer very loudly. It could be very violent, though. In day-to-day life, people went to public baths to wash, exercise, relax, and see their friends. The baths had hot, warm, and cold rooms. Some baths had gardens or libraries. People prayed to a lot of gods in the temples. People liked to see plays and listen to music. They also liked to hear stories. Some shops would close at noon due to the heat. People would eat a simple meal of bread, olives, cheese, and beans. In the evening the streets would come alive again. Some people had lamps in their homes. It could be very dangerous on the dark streets. Although life in Rome was different for the rich and poor, it was all about family, work, religion, entertainment, and community. Living in Rome was not easy, but there were baths, markets, and great buildings. It was very exciting.

Lab Report Summary - Affect of salt on the boiling point of water

In this lab we are trying to determine if the boiling point of water will change if we add salt. We used 500ml of water. We used a thermometer to measure the temperature. We first heated up our water without salt. We looked at what the temperature is when it starts to boil. The boiling point of the water is about 100 degrees C. That's pretty much the normal boiling point of water. Then, we added two tablespoons of salt to another 500ml of water. We mix it so that the salt dissolves in the water. We then heat the water. When the salt water starts to boil, we look at the temperature. It is about 101 degrees C.

The amount of boiling point went up by 1 degree C about. This is because the particles from the salt when dissolved make it harder for the water to evaporate to air. So the water has to reach a bit of a higher temperature in order to boil. So this supports our hypothesis. The boiling point of the salt water was higher then the water by its self.

There could've been some errors like maybe we didn't read the thermometer right or we didn't measure the salt right. We didn't have exact same heating conditions. Maybe not all of the salt actually dissolved. But this experiment shows that the salt makes the boiling point go up. But not by much.

In the ancient Egypt, the pyramids were mostly constructed as tombs for the pharaohs (their kings). As the ancient Egyptians thought that life after death existed, the body and possessions of their rulers had to be secure. This is why food, clothes, jewelry, pieces of furniture and even boats were often put inside the pyramid. All those things were needed for the journey to the next life. Perhaps the pyramid had a shape of sun rays so that the king could reach the sky and the world of gods. The fact of building the pyramid underlined the pharaoh's authority and the structure of the Egyptian society. Thousands of workers, including professional builders and farmers, cooperated and managed to cut, transport and put in place heavy stones. For example, the Great Pyramid of Giza, which was constructed for Pharaoh Khufu, was made approximately 4,500 years ago. It was the highest human construction for many years. Even though pyramids were made as tombs for the kings, they also became a great symbol of Egyptian religion, engineering, cooperation and appreciation of their rulers' inheritance.

What was the Cuban Missile Crisis? Why did it happen? How long did it last?

The Cuban missile crisis occurred due to the conflict between the U.S. and the USSR during the Cold War. In 1959, Fidel Castro took control of Cuba and set up a communist government. He also formed a strong relationship with the Soviet Union. This was problematic for the US as communism was getting too close to their country. In April of 1961 there was a failed invasion at the Bay of Pigs. Exiles from Cuba who were supported by the United States tried to take over Castro's government. The failure of this operation made Castro's position even stronger, making him believe that the United States could try to invade again.

Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev had a variety of motivations for having nuclear missiles in Cuba. He wanted to support Castro. He also wanted to extend the Soviet influence into the Western Hemisphere. Additionally, he wanted to improve Soviet military position. The US already had nuclear missiles in Turkey and Italy, which was so close to Soviet land. If he had the missiles in Cuba he would be able to even out the balance of power. Khrushchev wanted to prove that the Soviets wouldn't be bullied by America.

The Cuban missile crisis lasted from October 16th to October 28th 1962. This was a total of 13 days. A lot was riding on this crisis but both sides didn't want nuclear war. The U.S. had discovered the missile sites through their surveillance planes. President Kennedy had to come up with a response that wouldn't make him look weak, or make him look like he would provoke an attack. Instead of bombing Cuba right away, Kennedy put a naval "quarantine" in place to stop more Soviet shipments. He also was secretly planning for military action. The naval "quarantine" bought time for diplomacy to take place, but it also helped escalate the tension.

The crisis lasted a long time due to miscommunication, delays, and it was hard to keep military forces under control. It would've been possible for a U.S. invasion to provoke Soviet retaliation. There was also nuclear weapons in Cuba that the leaders of the U.S. were unaware of, held by Soviet military commanders in Cuba. Eventually Khrushchev agreed to dismantle the missiles, but only if the U.S. promised publicly that they wouldn't invade Cuba. Khrushchev also wanted a secret agreement that the U.S. would remove their missiles from Turkey. Kennedy's reluctance and secret negotiations allowed them to find a solution where they could both compromise and that helped avoid this crisis becoming a nuclear war.

Photosynthesis is the process in which green plants make food. The main site of photosynthesis is in the leaves. The chloroplasts are small structures within plant cells. They are the site of photosynthesis. The chloroplasts are filled with a green pigment called chlorophyll. Chlorophyll is able to trap light energy from the Sun. This is the energy required for photosynthesis.

The carbon dioxide (CO2) required for photosynthesis enters the plant from the air via the small holes in the leaves (stomata). Water (H2O) enters the plant from the soil via the roots. The water is transported up the stem to the leaves via special tubes. The plant uses the light energy trapped by the chlorophyll and, via a series of chemical reactions, combines the carbon dioxide and water to form glucose and oxygen.

Glucose is a sugar. It is the plant's food. Glucose can be immediately used in respiration to provide energy for growth and life processes. Surplus glucose can be converted to starch. The starch can be stored in the roots, stems, fruits and seeds. Glucose is also used by plants to make cellulose. This is a substance which strengthens the cell walls of plants. Plants can also use glucose to make other substances that are required for a healthy growth.

Oxygen is a waste product of photosynthesis. It is given out into the atmosphere via the stomata. The oxygen produced is important because it is needed by humans and animals for respiration. Photosynthesis is therefore vital for almost all forms of life. It produces food and oxygen but removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.

The word equation for photosynthesis is:

carbon dioxide + water glucose + oxygen

This reaction requires light and chlorophyll. Photosynthesis is vital for the growth of plants. It is the starting point for many food chains. Life on Earth would not have enough food and oxygen if photosynthesis did not occur. This would mean that most life on Earth would cease to exist.

Gatsby is a tragic hero. He is a tragic hero due to his extreme hope and loyalty to a certain ideal that he makes a detrimental mistake of mistaking a past dream as real life. Even though Gatsby's money is from illegal activities and his love for Daisy is somewhat of an illusion his passion to believe in a bright future ahead is what makes his tragic end painful.

The green light symbolizes Gatsby's desire for Daisy as well as his desire for this future he has with Daisy. The light at first seems to be obtainable but is only separated by a body of water. This is the separation between Gatsby's dream and reality. The daisy is not the innocent girl he remembers anymore. And that the past cannot be revisited. But Gatsby does not want to accept that fact. Gatsby's tragic flaw is not his love for Daisy but it's his idealism. His belief that the lost time can be recovered by money and determination and faith. Gatsby telling Nick that the past can be repeated is a way for him to show his own dream's power over him.

Chapter 8 is the moment Gatsby's tragedy is complete. When Daisy is driving the car that hits and kills Myrtle. Gatsby stands outside Daisy's house to cover for her. He waits for her even when she says nothing. Wilson who is in mourning and wants revenge shoots Gatsby at his pool. Gatsby dies alone and still attached to the dream he pursues while Daisy is free from any responsibility. This comparison is what makes his death tragic. Gatsby gives his life for someone who's not willing to give up anything for him.

Gatsby like any tragic hero has a desire as well as a fatal flaw. The dream makes him great but his denial of reality is his demise. And his death shows the green light as not a guarantee that all dreams become true. It's the symbol of endless pursuit of a future that may not be attained. Gatsby is tragic as his hope is admirable but also ultimately leads to his death.

The importance of Brown vs. Board of Education.

Brown v. Board of Education, decided in 1954, is a landmark in Supreme Court history. Unanimously (9-0) the Supreme Court held on May 17, 1954 that segregation in public schools was unconstitutional. It reversed the 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson decision that allowed 'separate but equal' establishments. Segregated education was also unconstitutional by the 14th Amendment, Equal Protection Clause.

The case centered around the plight of Black children who were relegated to separate schools. Even if the schools were comparable, segregation in essence made Black children feel inferior and they were not given equal opportunity. This had educational and psychological disadvantages that were argued by Thurgood Marshall and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund. Chief Justice Earl Warren proclaimed that separate educational facilities were "inherently unequal".

The importance of a 9-0 decision has many aspects. First and foremost it carried a tremendous moral and legal weight. If there had been a split decision, many states may have been tempted to disregard the decision. But with a unanimous decision, it expressed that it was a Constitutional imperative that there be equality, whether people liked it or not. Secondly, it showed that the Federal government could stand up to state-sponsored racism. It gave a boost to the overall Civil Rights Movement. For example, the Montgomery Bus Boycott and subsequent fights for voting rights and public accommodation.

Although Brown was a momentous decision, it did not instantly make segregation disappear. There was much resistance by white authorities to desegregate. For some schools it would be years before it took place. Brown II was decided in 1955 where the Supreme Court said that it had to happen 'all deliberate speed'. However it was not easy to enforce it. Nevertheless, Brown set the nation's course in a new direction. It said that equality isn't just about having the same buildings and facilities. It's about giving equal dignity and equal opportunities. The fact that it was a unanimous 9-0 decision is a powerful statement. It is a powerful statement about the Supreme Court as protector of Constitutional rights. It is a powerful statement about American democracy. We can learn a lot from the legacy of Brown. It says that court decisions are important if we (the community, institutions, etc.) work together to turn principles into practice.

The aim of the experiment was to see if the period of the pendulum changes with the mass of the pendulum. The period is the time it takes for the pendulum to swing back and forth one time. We had the same length of the string (0.5 m). We used 2 masses, 50 g and 200 g. The period of pendulum was around 1.4 second for both cases.

Based on the results it seems that period didn't change much when the mass of the pendulum changed. This is within our experiment boundaries. This data is consistent with the pendulum equation: \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}\). This equation indicates that the period is mostly determined by the length of string and the value of gravity. The mass of the bob didn't seem to impact the period. The expected period for pendulum that has the 0.5 m length should be around 1.42 seconds. This is quite close to the number we got (1.4 seconds). So this data seems to confirm the scientific theory.

There are several possible errors in the experiment. One possible error was that we used stopwatch to measure the time for the pendulum to swing. This could lead to reaction time errors (especially when we started and stopped the timer). Another possible error was due to air resistance and/or friction at the support. Also the angle of release might have been a bit different every time. Maybe if the angle was too big, then the period might not have been close enough to the perfect equation. Another error could be that we only measured one or a few swings. That would decrease the reliability of the data.

There are a few ways in which the experiment can be improved. For example, we can measure 10 or 20 swings and divide total time by the number of swings. Also we can try to do a few measurements for each and then take the average. Basically it seems that the mass of the pendulum did not (or had little impact) on the period of pendulum if the length of string is constant.

Around the year 1440, Johannes Gutenberg invented the printing press. This revolutionized information in Europe as it made spreading written works quicker, more cost effective, and easier. In the past, most books were laboriously copied by hand, often by monks. This made books very valuable and scarce. Gutenberg invented a printing press with movable metal type and ink. This meant a single printer could create many pages all the same. This created the idea of a book industry and promoted literacy.

With the rise of books, ideas could spread internationally and across class boundaries. Scholars could then examine texts and build off of each other's research. The printing press helped to fuel the Renaissance as works of art, science, history, and ancient Greece and Rome were spread. Printing also allowed scientists like Copernicus and Vesalius to share their findings. Trade, navigation, and education benefited from better maps and manuals.

Religion and politics also shifted due to printing. Martin Luther's attacks on the Catholic Church could be spread with pamphlets to initiate the Protestant Reformation. Governments and religion were able to spread laws and beliefs more broadly, but also arguments could be printed to foster propaganda, rumors, and hate. With literacy rising, people started to challenge traditional sources and participate in arguments.

Yet this wasn't always fair. Women, the poor, and rural populations may not have had the same opportunities for education or books. Censorship could also happen as printers might be limited if a government was afraid of rebellions or criticisms. Still, society was forever changed. Information was able to spread more rapidly. Education and religious developments were reinforced. Modern science, politics, and culture were able to flourish. The biggest impact is that ideas had a broader audience.

Water Cycle- Water is continually moving through Earth's atmosphere and over its surface. Evaporation occurs when the Sun warms water, on the ocean, lakes, rivers, and puddles. The heat causes the liquid water to turn into an invisible gas called water vapor. The vapor travels up into the air. As the water vapor travels further up, into the cooler atmosphere it releases heat. Condensation happens when the vapor turns into small droplets of water. They cling to dust particles to make clouds. If a cloud has a lot of the droplets of water, or ice crystals. Then the cloud will release precipitation. The precipitation may come down as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. The water is now on Earth's surface again. In collection, water collects in the oceans, lakes, rivers, glaciers, or underground. Water is also absorbed by plants and consumed by animals. The sun heats up the water, which has been collected and then the cycle begins again. The water cycle produces fresh water to sustain living things. The cycle also affects the shape of the land. And helps regulate the Earth's temperature. Life would not last very long at all, on our planet without the water cycle.

The reason we have seasons is because the Earth's axis is titled at an angle of about 23.5 degrees as it orbits the Sun. Earth's tilted axis stays in roughly the same orientation as the Earth orbits. Different areas of Earth experience sunlight from different angles and different amounts of time depending on where the Earth is in its orbit. When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, it receives more direct sunlight. It's days are longer and the weather is warmer. This is the Northern Hemisphere's summer. On the other hand the Southern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun. It receives less direct sunlight, days are shorter and it experiences winter. Half a year later the Earth is at the opposite point of its orbit around the Sun. Now the Southern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun so it experiences summer. The Northern Hemisphere experiences winter. The Spring and Autumn seasons come in-between as neither the Northern nor Southern Hemisphere are strongly tilted toward or away from the Sun. While Earth is slightly closer to the Sun at one point in its orbit around the sun, the change in distance doesn't account for seasons. The angle of the sunlight and the amount of daylight hours are much more significant. The tilted axis of Earth and its yearly orbit around the Sun is what causes the seasonal pattern that we experience.

Should students have four day school weeks?

Yes, students should have a four day school week. A four day school week may help students in many ways. Their health will increase, they will get more learning, and they will get more family time. If students had a three day weekend they would get more time for rest, homework, and other activities. Many students are very tired when they have to wake up early for five straight days. With one extra day off school students may come back ready and focused to learn.

Teachers can benefit from having a four day school week. Teachers will have extra time to plan their lessons, grade homework, and not get burnt out. Teachers will be happier and the lessons might be more interesting. Family time is an amazing aspect that families can have. Also students can go to their appointments without having to miss school.

There are people who are concerned that students may get a longer day for school. The time for learning may be reduced with a shorter school week. This is a logical concern, but the schools could make up for it by increasing their day or they can use the fifth day as an optional time for tutoring, clubs, and meals. Schools can create child care programs for the families who need it.

The result show that there was an obvious effect of temperature on the yeast's rate of carbon dioxide production. The yeast made 18mL CO2 in 20 minutes at 35 degrees celcius, whereas it made 6mL CO2 at 15 degrees celcius. So at 35 degrees celcius the yeast made 0.9mL CO2 per minute, and at 15 degrees celcius the yeast made 0.3mL CO2 per minute. The yeast made 3 times the rate of carbon dioxide production at the higher temperature.

Yeast get energy from breaking down glucose. They do anaerobic respiration (fermentation) in conditions of low oxygen. This produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. Enzymes control the reaction. When you go from 15 degrees celcius to 35 degrees celcius the enzyme and substrate particles gain kinetic energy. They move faster, collide more and have more enzyme-substrate successful collisions. So more CO2 is released from fermentation at 35 degrees celcius because the rate of fermentation is faster.

At 15 degrees celcius the particles had less kinetic energy so less successful collisions and the enzymes were working slower. This is why there was less volume of carbon dioxide. But it does not show that the fermentation rate increases when it's hotter than 15 degrees celcius. If you increased the temperature above the optimum temperature for the yeast, eventually the enzymes would lose their shape which would make them respire less or even stop respiration. The optimum temperature for this yeast might be near 35 degrees celcius. But you would need to test a range of temperatures to find this out precisely.

There are variables that might of effected the experiment like amount/concentration of glucose, amount of yeast, pH, how accurate you were at measuring gas volume. To make this reliable you should repeat this investigation several times at each temperature and calculate a mean. You should use the same apparatus each time, same volumes, same yeast concentration, same amount of time. You could use a water bath to keep the same temperatures. And making sure there are no leaks in your apparatus to make CO2 measurements more accurate. So it does show that when it's warmer (but within the suitable range) the rate of yeast fermentation increases.

Social Media and Teenagers' Sleep

Social media has become a vital aspect of teenagers' lives. It has provided them a platform to communicate, express their thoughts and be up to date with current events. Nonetheless, using social media, particularly late at night, can have negative effects on teenagers' sleep. According to our class survey, 19 out of 27 students are using their phones past 12 midnight. This is a striking statistic indicating that the use of phones late at night is prevalent and could be affecting the students' health and academic performance.

One of the key issues with social media is the addictive nature of phone usage. Teenagers might start with the intention of checking just one message, but before they know it, they are scrolling through videos, posts, and comments for hours on end. Social media apps are crafted to keep users engaged, and it's easy to lose track of time. This often leads to teenagers getting less sleep than they should.

The light emitted from the phone screen might also impact sleep. The screen light can make the brain more alert, particularly when the phone is used near bedtime. Furthermore, the notifications, messages, and even online debates can trigger feelings of excitement, anxiety or stress in teenagers. This could disrupt their ability to unwind and get to sleep.

The consequences of poor sleep are numerous. Students might struggle with focus in class, memory retention and completing their homework when they're sleep deprived. They could also experience irritability or lack of motivation during the day. Over time, the

consistent lack of sleep can negatively affect their physical and mental well-being.

To mitigate these impacts, teenagers could implement a set time limit for their social media usage at night. They may consider keeping their phones out of the bed area, silencing notifications, or relying on an alarm clock rather than their phones. Educational institutions and families could also play a role in educating teenagers about healthy sleep practices.

In conclusion, while social media can be a valuable tool, its usage past 12 midnight can significantly compromise teenagers' sleep. Based on our class survey, this seems to be a common occurrence. By establishing limits and designating a no-screen time during bedtime, teenagers can improve their sleep quality and excel more in school.

$15 federal minimum wage

The federal minimum wage needs to increase to $15 per hour. Many full-time workers are struggling to make ends meet on the current minimum wage. Though it may present difficulties for certain businesses, an increase in the minimum wage would benefit society by lowering poverty, improving communities, and allowing workers to have a greater share of the wealth they contribute.

The federal minimum wage has stayed at $7.25 per hour since 2009. Full-time work at the current wage only yields roughly $15,000 per year before taxes. For many places across the country, that's not enough to pay for rent, food, transportation, healthcare and other necessities. No one should have to work 40 hours a week and still live in poverty or need public assistance. A higher minimum wage would allow millions to live and provide for their families with more dignity.

Some will say that a $15 wage would make it difficult for small businesses - they'd need to increase prices, cut hours, or even cut jobs. That's a valid point that should be considered, particularly in places where the cost of living is lower. But higher wages also benefit businesses. Higher pay often leads to more motivated workers who are less likely to leave their jobs. Fewer job turnovers will save businesses money on recruiting and training new employees. Plus, the increased income of employees leads them to spend more at local businesses, which contributes to a growing economy.

There's no one-size-fits-all wage that's ideal for every region, so perhaps a gradual implementation or coupling with local policies could be part of the solution. But the federal government still needs to set a baseline minimum standard. Nobody should be working full-time and not be able to afford necessities.

While a $15 federal minimum wage wouldn't fix all economic issues, it's an important step towards justice. With increased consumer spending and less poverty, it would lead to a more robust economy and a more equitable society.

How vaccines prepare the immune system
Vaccines prepare the body's immune system to recognize and respond to a pathogen (virus, bacteria, etc.) without getting the disease by introducing part or a form of the pathogen into the body. This can be a weakened or dead form of the pathogen or even just a protein, genetic instruction, or benign part of the pathogen. These pieces are known as antigens.

Upon introduction of the vaccine, the antigens are recognized as foreign by the immune system cells. This will kick-start the immune system, which is specific and can get better with practice. B cells play a role. Some of the B cells will differentiate to become plasma cells that produce antibodies. Antibodies are proteins that bind to the antigens of the pathogen. Antibodies can block or label the pathogen for destruction. This can prevent or reduce the severity of the infection by blocking or killing the pathogen.

Some of the activated B cells become memory B cells. Memory B cells stick around in the body after the vaccine is gone. They remember the antigen and can respond more quickly and robustly when they encounter the pathogen in the body again. The immune system may also generate memory T cells to assist with the coordination or killing of infected cells.

This immunological memory means that often a vaccinated individual can clear out the pathogen before it can grow enough to cause disease. Some vaccines need multiple doses or booster shots. This will build up the immune response each time and can keep the protection going as the memory cells and antibody levels fade with time. Vaccines typically do not prevent all infections but are highly effective at preventing severe disease and complications as well as transmission.

Vaccines also help with community protection. With lots of people being immune, there are less opportunities for the pathogen to transmit from one person to another. This also helps protect those that cannot get vaccinated. So vaccines can safely prepare the immune system to prepare against a first encounter with the antigen and can lead to a more rapid and effective response next time.

Cell phones are common in schools nowadays. These cell phones have become essential to many students as a way to stay connected to their parents, to find information or even to manage their assignments. Even though they are essential in some cases, they also have the potential to take away focus from their studies. Because of this, cell phones should be banned from school hours with some exceptions.

One reason cell phones should be banned from most school hours is because they can be a distraction. This is in the form of notifications, games, videos, social media and more. By banning these cell phones, schools can create a more peaceful and equal space for learning. For this reason, cell phones should be allowed in schools with the phones being off in their lockers or backpacks. Students should be able to use cell phones in approved emergencies. Teachers may also be able to use cell phones for certain learning activities if needed. A strict policy will help avoid confusion and provide equal treatment.

To summarize, cell phones should not be in charge of school days. By banning cell phone use during class time and breaks, students can preserve their focus and improve the behavior in classrooms. I broke it up into the two parts of the phone bill. There's the set fee per month of $25. That's a flat fee that you pay regardless of how many texts you send. I'm dividing by 0.10. What this is telling me is how many groups of 10 cents there are in 12 dollars. So 12 divided by 0.10. It equals 120. So t = 120. That means that 120 texts were sent.

Just to double check my answer I plug 120 in for t in the original equation. So that would be the cost for the texting part. 120 x $0.10 = $12. Add on the set flat cost and I get $25 + $12 = $37. Lowering Voting Age to 16

Should voting age be lowered to 16 years old? Currently, many countries require citizens to be 18 years old to vote. However, there are many people who think that 16 year-olds should be allowed to vote. Austria set an example of this when they lowered voting age to 16 in 2007. This is a thought that deserves consideration for democracies.

Lowering voting age to 16 has its good points. One of the good points about this is that 16 year-olds are impacted by political decisions, including decisions on education, climate change, public transport, and privacy. By allowing them to vote, this might motivate them to be knowledgeable about these topics and take part in democracy. Another good point is that young people should have a say in decisions that impact their future.

Some people oppose lowering voting age to 16. These people think that many 16 year-olds may not be knowledgeable or mature enough to make good decisions. They may simply go with their parents, friends, or social media influencers. Another reason they might think 18 is better is that voting involves understanding complex topics such as taxes, international relations, and economy. Therefore, they feel like 18 is a more appropriate age because young adults will be more independent.

Personally, I think that voting age should be lowered to 16 but with the help of schools in preparing the students. Students should be taught about elections, how to find trustworthy sources, and how to distinguish misinformation through civics lessons. What Austria has shown since 2007 is that younger people can be a part of a democracy. While it doesn't mean that every teenager will make wise votes by lowering the age to 16, neither does being 18. But it shows that there's consideration of what is important to the young people and also encourages them to become responsible citizens. 16 year-olds can be an asset to society as long as they're educated.

Learning to Play When Life Knocks You Down

I was sure that missing out on basketball season was going to be the hardest part after breaking my wrist. But once the cast was on, I realized that it was not the basketball. The most frustrating part was that I could not play my guitar. I had been self taught for two years now. The guitar is my safe haven. Anytime I was overwhelmed or just felt stuck I would turn to the guitar.

But now I couldn't make chords. I couldn't strum. My wrist was immobilized. I stayed away from the guitar. I thought that missing out for a few months wouldn't be a big deal. But every time I saw my guitar in the corner of my room it was just a reminder that I was missing out. So I avoided it because it made it seem like a bigger problem than it actually was.

But then my physical therapist told me that I should be more focused on the progress I was making, not perfection. So I started with listening to songs and looking at the chord diagrams. Once my doctor gave me permission to move around, I started just working on moving each individual finger. I started with easier songs. I tried to change my hand positioning. I changed how I was using my pick. Sometimes I would play for 10 minutes and just gain the slightest bit of progress. But it was progress nonetheless.

It was not some big breakthrough. It was deciding to try again even though my wrist hurt. Even though I sounded really awkward. Until I finally played a whole song for my family. It was really simple but it felt important. I had re-established my confidence and strength.

That's what I learned from breaking my wrist. It's not about going back to normal. It's about being resilient and adapting. Now when I'm overwhelmed with school work or life's setbacks I break it down into smaller tasks. I ask for help. I wait for progress and be patient. And I still play the guitar. But I face the challenges in a new way. I may have limitations, but that does not change the outcome. It just changes the approach.

Our statistic project was centered around the amount of time spent doing homework in a normal school night. We surveyed 60 students in our grade with a small, anonymous questionnaire. We asked them to fill out the number of minutes typically spent doing homework in each student. We told them that it was a voluntary participation and that we were not asking for names or anything like that. Once we collected all of the data we put it from least to greatest. Then we put it into a frequency table and a box and whisker plot.

The most important thing we got from the data was the median: 75 minutes. Since we had 60 answers we took the median by seeing where the 30th and 31st place are and we take the average of them. To calculate the area of a circle, you use the formula: A = πr², where A is the area, r is the radius and π is a number which is roughly 3.14. The radius of a circle is the distance from the center to the outside of the circle. In this case the radius is 4 centimeters, so we replace the r with 4: A = π4² Now let's square the radius. 4² = 16 Now let's multiply. A = 16π square centimeters. Now let's use the number 3.14 for π. So 16 times 3.14 = 50.24. So the area of this circle is about 50.24 square centimeters. We use π because all circles have the same relationship between circumference and diameter. This relationship is called π. And it's always the same, regardless of how big or small the circle is. This formula works because you can divide a circle into a bunch of thin slices. And they all look like a rectangle when put together like this. The length and width are roughly the radius and half the circumference.

The Pythagorean theorem describes how the three sides of any right triangle relate to each other. The theorem says that in a right triangle (a right angle), the relationship between the two sides that make the right angle (the legs) and the third side (the side across from the right angle - called the hypotenuse) is a² + b² = c².

To understand this, consider a right triangle where the legs are 3 units long and 4 units long. The hypotenuse is 5 units long. The area of the square made from the 3 unit side is 3² = 9 square units. The area of the square made from the 4 unit side is 4² = 16 square units. So the total area of the two squares is 25 square units. The area of the square made from the 5 unit hypotenuse side is 5² = 25 square units. So the area of the two small squares equals the area of the large square. 9 + 16 = 25.

This isn't just a coincidence. If you take 4 copies of this right triangle and put them in a square, you'll notice that there's a space left over. But there's two different ways you can arrange that space left over. The 4 triangles have the same area in either case. Now, look at the leftover spaces. You'll see that the area of the square that makes the hypotenuse is the same as the combined area of the squares made from the legs of the triangle. So this holds for any right triangle. Even for the 3 - 4 - 5 right triangle.

You get off with the pilot's body. The plane went down in a lake so deep you couldn't find the bottom, and you spent the first night just trying to get the wreck out. You get a lot of mileage out of a cowrie shell. Ralph and Piggy find one on the beach and start blowing it to get the other boys together. That's how they got the first meeting off the ground. They made a deal that you only got to talk if you were holding the thing. It was a pretty decent shot at democracy, and for a while Ralph got away with it. The whole arrangement held together so long as the boys kept buying into it. They stopped buying in pretty fast. Jack would barge in, ignore the rule, and push the group toward hunting. Rescue and cooperation got dropped in the process.

The shell wore out in the same way the boys did. It went from being a useful and pretty thing to something battered. That last bit is the part that gets you. Roger swings the boulder, takes out Piggy, and smashes the conch in the same stroke. Piggy was the one left to think things through, and the shell was what kept that thinking from getting hurt. With both of them gone the whole setup went with them. You can put together all the rules you want. None of it is going to hold unless people actually want to follow it. That is the whole of Golding's point.

You get a hatchet out of your mother's hands and you're in the air by yourself. That's the setup for the first three chapters of Gary Paulsen's *Hatchet*. You're thirteen, headed to your father's place up in the Canadian wilderness. You've got plenty to be angry about, mostly the whole thing that got your parents to this point. You keep going over "the Secret" in your head, that thing you know about your mother and another man. The pilot is enough of a sport to show you the radio and let you take the controls for a bit. Then his heart gives out. You're left with a dead man in the front seat and a plane that won't do what you tell it. You call out on the radio and get nothing back but static. The only way out is to get that thing down, and the only place to do it is a lake. You end up in the water.

You kept every one of the things that mattered. The pilot's instructions are the only thing standing between you and the ground, and you have to trust that. The crash isn't some clean thing either. You just get the plane down and hope the water takes the worst of the hit. From that point on you've got the hatchet and nothing else to work with.

You get the conch working on the first day out, and that's when the whole thing gets set. It's the only thing that keeps a bunch of scared little kids from tearing each other apart. When you blow it you get a right to talk, and nobody else gets to cut in. That's about the most you can get out of a group of people who've lost their parents. It doesn't actually stop the fighting, it just puts a lid on it for a while. The beast they are all so scared of never actually shows up in any form you could get a grip on. The thing that gets them in the end is the stuff they carry around inside.

Once that thing gets smashed the whole arrangement they had goes with it. You can't put a lid on the worst of people with a bit of coral. The thing that used to keep the noise in check stops working the moment it gets broken. You end up with the sort of thing that gets you killed. It was never going to be a permanent cure for the sort of trouble they were in. The whole setup they got going was only ever a very thin thing to begin with.

You end up having to rely on the sort of rules that people will only keep up as long as they find it convenient to do so. Once that convenience runs out the whole thing just falls apart. It was never going to hold out against what was already there. The thing they had to rely on for any sort of order simply wasn't strong enough to keep the worst of it from getting out.

You should just keep the salad bar. 140 of us hit it up last week, which says plenty about whether it's worth the money. You get lettuce, carrots, tomatoes, cucumbers, beans, and fruit there. That's real vitamins to get you through the afternoon, and you can take as much or as little as you want. A lot of us have to watch for allergies and the hot line doesn't let for that. You also get to eat something different instead of the same old hot meals. Nobody is going to try a new vegetable if it isn't right in front of them.

You'll hear that it's too expensive or that it just ends up in the trash. You can get ahead of the waste by watching what people actually take and handing out smaller containers. Take the bar away and you've got a whole lot of unhappy students. Those 140 of us who used it last week are a pretty clear sign of what the rest of the school wants.
