You get three minutes to get ready, which is about as much time as you need to fall apart. I stood in the school gym in my too big basketball uniform, the fabric riding up every time I shifted my weight. The whole seventh grade was out there, and the noise they made got so loud it was hard to think. That was the part I'd been dreading all week. My old team had been so much better that I kept comparing myself to them. When the coach finally called my name, my legs went out from under me. I made the first three shots, which got the crowd to settle down. Then I missed the next two, and I could see the faces of my old teammates in the crowd. I stopped trying to be that better player I'd lost and just started playing. It wasn't a great game, but I got through it. The whole thing took less than an hour. Still, that three minute wait in the corner felt like it would go on forever. You end up learning a lot about yourself in that sort of situation. The lesson I got out of it was that you can't get back to being that other person. You just have to get on with the game you are in.

You talk a big game the night before. I told the whole team I was set. Walking into that gym took all that talk and set it aside. The lights were too bright for the polished floor and the crowd got so loud it sounded like thunder. The ball kept slipping out of my hands. I could barely get a grip.

Coach got us in a huddle and told us to take a deep breath and just think about the first play. I tried. The breathing part worked out, the pounding in my chest didn't. The whistle went off and I just stood there. Then the opening pass I had run hundreds of times came back to me. I got to my spot and threw it to Maya. She put it in and the whole team let out a cheer.

That got me moving. I even managed to steal the ball near the end of the second quarter. The final score had us ahead by two points. It was more about finding out that the nerves didn't mean I hadn't prepared. They just meant the game was worth something to me. That's what I go back to when I get anxious. I take a breath, remember the work I put in, and just make that first move.

You end up using the fear to get something done. That's the whole of it. Courage isn't some state of being perfectly calm. You are just playing with your knees still shaking.

You can't afford to kill the salad bar. Last week 140 of us used it, and that isn't some rounding error. That's more than the whole 8th grade combined. You've got to be looking at the wrong numbers if you think that kind of a crowd isn't worth keeping around. The bar also does something the hot line never has. It lets kids actually put together a meal they like. You get a lot of complaints that the regular offerings are too heavy, and the salad bar is the only real way to get around that. Take it away and you are left with a whole lot of people who have nowhere to go for a light meal.

The cost of running it is nothing next to the trouble of getting a whole new group of students to eat. Those 140 people will not simply switch to the hot line. They will probably just skip lunch. That is a result nobody around here wants to see. Keep the thing running. It has already proved itself to be something people actually want to use. The figures from last week are there for anyone to look at. All that is left is for the people in charge to act on what the students have already made so plain.

You get the whole story through Ponyboy Curtis, a greaser who keeps getting in trouble with the rich Sideburns. He writes it all down to prove his people aren't the bad guys the movies make them out to be. The whole thing changes for him after he and Johnny run off to a ranch in the hills. That's where they get caught in a church fire. Johnny goes back in to get some little kids out and ends up with some pretty bad burns. He hangs on long enough to give Ponyboy that last bit of advice, which is to stay gold. That phrase is a reference to a Robert Frost poem that was in a book they were reading. Frost is talking about how people lose some of their innocence as they get older. Johnny wants Pony to keep that part of himself from getting ground down by the world.

The ending has a way of tying that whole thing together. When Ponyboy finally gets around to writing his story, he finds out that other kids are reading it. They see things in the book that they themselves have felt. That gets across the one thing the two groups have been missing all along. They aren't so different after all. The book ends up saying that you can tell a lot about a person by the way he looks at the sunset. It is the same sunset no matter which side of the street you happen to be on. You don't have to be a greaser or a Sideburn to see it.

You get the whole thing in a few pages. Hinton wrote it back in 1967 and it's still mostly about a 14 year old named Ponyboy. He's a Greaser, which means he's stuck in a running fight with the Socs, the rich kids from the other side of town. Ponyboy reads books and stops to look at sunsets. That sets him off from the rest of his crew. His friend Johnny is a different case. The boy is scared to death by the beating he gets at home. Then the Socs corner the two of them and Johnny ends up killing Bob. That puts the pair on the run, and they end up holeing up in an old church.

The church burns down on them. They get a bunch of kids out and the whole thing makes them out to be heroes. It doesn't save Johnny though. He dies in the hospital and that's what finally gets through to Ponyboy. You can't get out of the mess you make by making more of it. Johnny had told him to stay gold, a line he pulled out of Robert Frost's "Nothing Gold Can Stay." That gold is the innocence and goodness that gets worn off as you get older. Johnny wanted him to keep some of it.

It works because the kids in it aren't some made up types. You find the same fears and dreams in the Socs that you do in the Greasers. Nobody in the book gets off by looking at a person's social group. That's the part that still hits. You get a story that's pretty grim and still manages to get you to see someone else's side.

I used to read The Road Not Taken as some kind of individualist's hymn. Guy in a yellow wood, two paths, pick one. You can't go back so the choice has to count for something. That part got to me. I kept wondering what I'd have gotten if I'd gone the other way. Then I went back and looked at what the speaker actually says. The roads were "really about the same." Neither one had been more trampled. Both were covered in leaves and both looked just as good. That flatly contradicts the closing line about taking "the one less traveled by." You keep hearing the confident part and missing the joke. Frost never once shows that one road was the braver or better bet.

That future "sigh" he talks about doesn't settle things either. It might be content or it might be a regret he hasn't quite named. He pictures himself spinning the whole thing out "ages and ages hence," which is to say he's already letting memory get hold of it. The heroic version of the tale is something he's going to make up. The roads never actually differed to begin with.

So I don't get out of the poem some lesson about bucking the crowd. What I get is a pretty plain statement that we make our choices mean something after the fact. You can't line up the life you got against the one you passed up and call the comparison a fact. The last two lines aren't there to pump you up. They're there to make you look at how sure you are of your own story.

You've probably heard the ending in a graduation speech. The speaker took the road less traveled and it made all the difference, which is why we keep handing out copies of the poem. That version isn't in the last two lines. The whole trick is the first line of the final stanza where he says he took the one that looked like it had more wear. He goes on to say that in the way they lay in the grass the two roads were in reality pretty much the same. He's telling you he made a choice out of a set of options that were essentially equal. The difference he ends up with is the one he tells the story to create. You have to go back and look at the whole thing to see that the roads were almost equally worn and that the speaker knew he would probably never get back to try the other one. The poem is about the human need to make our own past seem like the product of some special and decisive act. It is a pretty clear eyed look at how we rewrite our own history. The roads were in fact very nearly the same and the story of one being more special is something the speaker makes up after the fact. You get that from the way he keeps saying he was going to keep the first road for another day. That day never comes and so the tale of the more romantic choice gets to grow. Frost is being very straight with you about the whole thing if you are willing to read what he actually wrote. The speech writers have just been very busy filling in the gaps he left for you to find.

That gets you to a little over three hundred words. You might want to cut the last sentence to get it in. It doesn't really add anything to the argument you have already made. The whole point is that the poem was never the inspirational thing people have made it out to be.

You're alone on stage in Act 2, Scene 1. Macbeth looks at the thing in front of him and asks, "Is this a dagger which I see before me?" He can't tell if it's some kind of supernatural sign or just his own overactive imagination. He wants to do the job and he's scared of it at the same time. He reaches out, saying, "Come, let me clutch thee," and finds there is nothing to grab. That gap between the image and the empty air is where his whole mess lives. The thing seems to lead him off, and when he names it a "fatal vision" he's naming both the death to come and the path he's already set.

He sees "gouts of blood" on the blade that aren't there. That's Duncan's murder getting worked out in his head before it happens. The whole scene is full of "night" and "witchcraft" to keep the mood threatening. He does end up putting the blame on his own "heat-oppressed brain" though. The long, doubtful sentences of the first part give way to something much shorter. "I go, and it is done" is all you get at the end. That's the point of the whole thing. Ambition has finally pushed past the rest of what he is. You end up feeling sorry for the fear in him, but you also see exactly how that sort of thing gets a person into such a mess.

You can't get to 1939 without going through 1919. The whole thing came down to how the victors handled the defeated German state. They made the country sign a peace that read more like a sentence than a settlement. Article 231 is the part everyone remembers, since it put the whole responsibility for the war on Germany's shoulders. That wasn't just a legal technicality. It gave the other nations a moral cover to take a huge share of the country's resources. The war reparations that followed from that article ended up strangling the German economy. You had to print off enormous amounts of money to keep up with the payments, which in turn wrecked the currency. The resulting hyperinflation wiped out the savings of ordinary people and left a deep sense of national humiliation.

That humiliation did a lot of work for later political agitators. You got a whole generation that had grown up hearing that the old order had been destroyed by outside forces. People were ready to listen to anyone who promised to get rid of the so called diktat. The economic misery gave that kind of talk a very concrete foundation to build on. When you add in the way the new borders had been drawn, you end up with a set of grievances that were almost impossible to settle through ordinary political means. The treaty had set the stage for all of that to happen. It had created the very conditions that made a second and much more destructive war possible. The whole sequence of events from 1919 onward had been written into the terms of that first peace.

You can't get around the war guilt clause. Article 231 of the 1919 treaty said Germany and its allies started the first war. That was a hard pill for most Germans to swallow. They figured the whole thing was more complicated than that, and the fact that their own government signed off on it only made them distrust the lot. You had a country primed for someone to come along and promise to wipe the whole thing off the books.

That someone was Hitler. He made a point of attacking the treaty on every front. But he had a lot of help from the thing itself. The reparations it demanded bled the German economy dry. You got debt, mass unemployment, and the kind of inflation that wiped out savings. When the government went and printed off huge amounts of money in 1923, it just finished the job. Families woke up to find they had nothing. You can argue that other things played a part, but the payments gave the whole thing a very concrete shape to be angry about.

They also got kicked out of a lot of their own territory and had to give up the bulk of their fighting power. No air force, no submarines, an army kept in check. That sort of thing makes a lot of people feel they've been surrounded and disrespected. Hitler's whole pitch was to get all of that back. The message got through because so many people were desperate to see the restrictions go.

It wasn't the only thing that got the country to that point. The Great Depression and the way other countries failed to act also had a lot to do with it. Still, you have to reckon with the part the treaty played. It handed the nationalists the very grievances they needed to get to power.

You get a pretty good read on where Macbeth's head is at once he starts talking to that knife. The whole thing hinges on the fact that he can't make up his mind about what he's seeing. He tells himself it's a real thing, a sign from the other side, and then he tries to convince himself it's just his own fevered brain at work. That back and forth is the whole point. A person in their right mind would either dismiss the thing or take it seriously, not keep flipping between the two. The fact that he keeps trying to grab it and keep missing it just underlines how far he's gotten from any sort of solid footing.

You also get a sense that he's been working himself into this frame of mind for quite some time. The whole business with the witches has left him in a state where he is ready to take any little thing as a green light. He has already made up his mind about the end result and is now just looking for some sort of outside confirmation to get him to act. The thing that frightens him most isn't the murder he is planning but the way his own mind has gotten so badly tangled up in it.

That the thing he is seeing should be able to lead him on and then vanish is a pretty good measure of the sort of mental state he has got himself into. He has lost the ability to tell what is real from what he has merely imagined. By the time he gets to the point of actually carrying out the deed, the line between what is in his head and what is actually out there has all but disappeared. That loss of any sure grip on the world is where the real horror of the whole thing lies.

You've got the short version of it, but the real fight started way back. Parliament kept trying to raise money from the colonies, and the colonists kept saying no. They figured out that they had no say in the making of these laws. The whole thing got off to a bad start with the Stamp Act of  1765. That one put a tax on everything from newspapers to playing cards. It wasn't the amount of the tax that got people so mad, it was the fact that they had to pay it to a government they had no representation in. The act got repealed, which only made the next round of trouble seem even worse.

Things kept getting worse until they finally boiled over in 1773. That was the year of the Boston Tea Party, when a bunch of colonists got together and dumped a whole shipload of taxed tea into the harbor. They figured that if they had to take a stand for their rights, they might as well do it in a way that was hard to ignore. The British response to that was to close the port of Boston and to tighten their grip on the whole of New England. That last move was the one that finally convinced most of the colonies that they had to break away. You could argue that without that specific series of acts and counter acts, the final break would never have happened.

You'd be in an insula, a packed apartment block, unless you had the money for a domus. Either way you were up early to get bread, fish, or what the markets had that day. Kids got different breaks. The rich ones sat in for reading and math, the rest picked up what they needed at home. You could always get out of the routine to see what the Colosseum was up to. That place opened in 80 AD and filled up with people watching gladiators and animal hunts. The cheering got pretty loud, and the fights got pretty bloody.

You'd end up at the public baths on an ordinary day. They had the hot, warm, and cold rooms you'd expect, and a few of them threw in a garden or a library. That was the same as your trip to the temples to pray to the gods. You got your share of plays and music along with it. The heat would shut the shops down around noon, so you'd eat a meal of bread, olives, cheese, and beans. The streets picked up again in the evening. Lamps got you through some of it, but you still had to watch out for the dark. The whole thing ran on family, work, and the crowd you moved with. It was a hard life, but the markets and the big buildings kept it from getting boring.

You get the short version if you look at the French and Indian War. That thing wrapped up in 1763 and left Britain with a debt to pay off. Parliament figured the colonies should chip in, and the colonists flatly refused. They had nobody elected to sit in that house, so they said the whole arrangement was illegal. You've heard the slogan they cooked up, no taxation without representation. It wasn't just a slogan. It was the whole of their case.

That case got a real test with the Stamp Act of 1765. You had to buy a stamp for newspapers, legal papers, licenses, and about every other printed thing you used. You got back at the law with speeches, with boycotts, and with your fists. Parliament gave in and repealed the act. They didn't give up the claim that they could tax you in the first place.

Things only got worse from there. More taxes rolled in, duties on tea chief among them, and Britain sent over soldiers to keep the peace. That made a lot of people feel like they were under military control. The whole thing came to a head in 1770 with the Boston Massacre, where British soldiers killed five colonists. You can't unsee that.

Then in 1773 Parliament handed the British East India Company a big leg up on the tea trade. The colonists took that as a fresh tax and a fresh threat. On December 16 of that same year a bunch of them got aboard the ships in Boston and put hundreds of chests of tea into the harbor. The Boston Tea Party was that, and nothing more.

Britain answered by locking down Massachusetts. The Intolerable Acts shut Boston Harbor and took away a good bit of the local government. You might have expected that to scare the rest of the colonies into line. It did the opposite and got them to band together. That distrust kept building until the colonies had a Continental Congress and were out fighting for independence in 1775.

You'd probably get up before the sun to beat the heat. Most of the neighborhood lived in tall insulae that were more likely to catch fire than to keep you warm. You might stop at a thermopolium for a hot meal since your own kitchen was little more than a brazier. The day's real entertainment waited in the great public baths. You could spend hours there washing off the city's grime, playing ball, or listening to some friend read aloud. If you were lucky you might get a pass to the Colosseum. That huge ring had only been open for a few years when you were born. The first games in the year 80 AD had shown off the whole of the empire to a screaming crowd. You'd see gladiators fight out there, and wild beasts brought from far off lands. The whole city seemed to gather for that sort of spectacle. When the sun got too strong you'd head back to the baths to cool off. That came to be the regular rhythm of your life. It was a world where the grandest public works stood right next to the most squalid of private dwellings. You had to take both of them in to get the whole picture of the place you called home.

That comes in at 218 words, so you can cut the last two sentences if you need to hit the limit. You might also want to check with your teacher on how much detail they want about the games. Some of them get pretty picky about that sort of thing.

You've got the whole thing in 1962. Castro had been running a communist shop in Cuba since 1959 and was getting pretty close to the Soviets. That set off alarms in Washington, and the failed Bay of Pigs invasion in April 1961 only made things worse. The exiles the U.S. backed got beaten, which told Castro the next American move would be a full scale attack. Khrushchev figured he could stop that by putting nuclear missiles on the island. It was also a way to answer the missiles the U.S. had already set up in Turkey and Italy. You can't really call that an unfair balance.

Once the U.S. spy planes got a look at the sites the whole thing got locked in for thirteen days, 16 to 28 October 1962. Kennedy had to pick something that wouldn't look like weakness or start a shooting war. He went with a naval quarantine to stop more Soviet shipments while the military got ready for the worst. That sort of held the situation open for the diplomats to get to work. You had to add in the slow and often garbled messages going back and forth. American commanders didn't know that Soviet officers on the ground had nuclear weapons. Khrushchev finally got out of it by trading the missiles for a public noninvasion pledge and a quiet deal to get the U.S. out of Turkey. Both of them got to save face and the whole thing stopped short of a nuclear exchange.

You've got three things tangled together. First there was the Bay of Pigs, which Khrushchev never forgot. That fiasco made the Soviet leader feel he had to put something in Cuba to keep the US from trying again. You add in the US Jupiter missiles sitting in Turkey and you get the whole picture of what he was after. He wasn't trying to start a war so much as he was trying to level the playing field. The whole thing was his way of saying the balance of power had to change.

That balance is also what kept the thing from getting out of hand. Both sides knew that a single mistake would end everything. You can see this in the back and forth of the secret letters between the two leaders. Those letters got them to the point of backing off. The public blockade you read about was really just a way to get them to that point. The 13 days you have in the history books were mostly a long and very careful process of trying to find a way out.

You also have to look at what each side was willing to give up. The US got the missiles out of Cuba while the Soviets got a promise that the same thing wouldn't happen in Turkey. Nobody really got everything they had wanted out of it. The whole affair just happened to work out because neither side wanted to take the final step. It was as much a matter of luck as it was of any kind of clever planning. That is the part of the story the later accounts tend to leave out.

You get 100°C out of 500 mL of plain water. That's the whole first run. The thermometer didn't lie and neither did the water. We then took a fresh 500 mL sample and dumped two tablespoons of salt in it. Stirring got the salt to dissolve, more or less. The second batch came to a boil at about 101°C. So you're looking at a 1°C jump. The salt particles get in the way of water molecules trying to get into the air, and the water has to get a bit hotter to get out. That's the whole mechanism and it's why the saltwater outlasted the plain stuff.

You can get this much wrong in a few ways. A bad read on the thermometer will get you. So will a sloppy measure of the salt. You might have used a different heat source for the two runs or you might have been left with some undissolved salt. The effect is there though. It's just a small one.

You put 500 mL of water in a beaker and got it to a rolling boil. It hit 100 C, which is the usual number for the place you live. That first run was just to get a baseline. You let the water cool, then stirred in two tablespoons of table salt. The water took longer to get going the second time. When it finally started to boil it was running at 101 C. That extra degree is the salt doing its thing. You kept the volume of the water the same both times so the only thing that changed was the amount of salt in it. The thermometer you used was accurate to a tenth of a degree so that one degree jump is a real result. It lines up with what you read in the textbook about adding a nonvolatile solute to a liquid. You did the whole thing twice to make sure you had not gotten a fluke reading. The two trials gave you the same final temperature.

You have to be a little careful about how much you stir in though. You used a fairly large amount of salt for that little bit of water. You might have gotten a bigger jump in the temperature if you had kept adding more. For the purpose of this exercise though the change was easy to see and record. The whole thing took well under an hour to get through. You ended up with a set of numbers that shows the effect pretty clearly. That is about all you can say from the data you got.

They were tombs. That's the main thing. You put the king in with his food, clothes, jewelry, and furniture. Sometimes you threw in a boat too. The whole thing rests on the idea that the dead guy still had a journey to make. The shape of the thing might be a shot at the sun, a way to get the guy up into the sky with the gods. You get a pretty good idea of how that society was organized by looking at the work. You need thousands of people, skilled builders and farmers alike, to cut and set those huge stones.

You can see the results at Giza. That's where they put Khufu. The place is about 4,500 years old and it kept the top spot as the tallest human made structure for a very long time. You end up with a monument that outlasted the king it was meant to serve. It stands there as a record of the religion, the engineering, and the plain respect those people had for their rulers.

They were mostly about getting the king to the afterlife. You have to remember that the Egyptians were convinced the dead Pharaoh would keep on ruling from there. That whole process needed a body that was ready for it, and the pyramid was the machine to keep it safe. They packed in enough gold and food to last forever. The shape itself wasn't just for looks either. The Egyptians figured out that the four sides pointed to the four corners of the world. That got the king up to the sky in the morning when the sun came out. You can still see the whole thing standing after 4,500 years. That's a lot longer than any other building they put up. It worked out pretty well for the people who put it together. They just had to get every single one of those blocks in the right place.

You have a little over 150 words there so you might want to cut the last two sentences. The bit about the gold and the shape of the thing is probably your strongest stuff. If your teacher wants you to sound more like you are explaining it to a friend that is the way to go. You might also want to check the part about the four sides since that is a bit of a simplification. It does get the main idea across though.

You've got it mostly right in the leaves. That's where the chloroplasts are, and the chloroplasts are stuffed with chlorophyll. The green stuff soaks up light from the sun. That light is the whole engine. You get the other two ingredients from the ground and the air. Stomata in the leaves let carbon dioxide in, and the roots pull water up the stem in special tubes. Once you've got all three, the plant runs them through a set of chemical reactions. Out the other end you get glucose and oxygen.

That glucose is the plant's food. It burns off in respiration to give the plant the energy it needs to get by. Anything left over gets turned into starch and stashed away in the roots, stems, or fruit. Some of it goes into making cellulose for the cell walls. The oxygen is just a waste product the plant doesn't need. It goes out through the same stomata the carbon dioxide came in on. You and every other animal are entirely dependent on that waste.

You can write the whole thing out as carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. You have to have the light and the chlorophyll for it to work. It is the first link in nearly every food chain you'll find. Most of the life on this planet would be out of business without it.

You've got the whole thing going on in the leaves. The green stuff you see, chlorophyll, is the main actor here. It soaks up light energy from the sun, mostly the red and blue parts of the spectrum. That light gets put to work in a set of reactions that end up splitting water. You're getting that water from the roots, and it moves up through the plant. When the light hits the chlorophyll the water molecules get broken apart. You get oxygen out of that process, which is why you get so much of it from forests. That oxygen just gets released back into the air.

The other half of the business is what happens with the carbon dioxide you get from the outside. That gas gets in through little openings in the leaf called stomata. The energy you got from the light gets used to fix that carbon into a form the plant can use. That form is glucose, a pretty basic sugar. The plant keeps some of that around for its own energy needs and it builds the rest of itself out of the stuff. You get the rest of the plant, the stems and the rest of the leaves, from that first bit of sugar.

You end up with a pretty neat trade. You put in some light, water, and carbon dioxide. You get out the sugar the plant needs to keep going along with a fair bit of the oxygen you and the rest of the animal world need to get by. The whole thing is what keeps the atmosphere in the shape it is.

You can get the whole story in a single line. On May 17, 1954, the Supreme Court went 9–0 to say that keeping Black and white kids in separate public schools was unconstitutional. That one vote killed *Plessy v. Ferguson* (1896) and the separate but equal idea it had blessed. The Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause had to cover these schools after all. The whole thing grew out of what those Black children were actually facing. You could put them in technically similar buildings, but the act of separating them stamped them as inferior. Thurgood Marshall and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund pressed that point, arguing the system did real psychological and educational damage. Chief Justice Earl Warren put it in the opinion by calling separate facilities "inherently unequal."

That 9–0 count did something a split decision never could. It took away the excuse for states to sit on the ruling. It also showed that the federal government could get in and break up state sponsored racism. The Montgomery Bus Boycott and the later push for voting rights and public accommodations all fed off that energy. You can't get that from a 5–4 vote.

None of it happened on schedule though. White officials fought the order and a lot of schools stayed segregated for years. The follow up, *Brown II* (1955), told the states to move with "all deliberate speed," a phrase that did very little to speed things up. The case still set the legal direction for the country. It got the courts to say that equality is about more than matching up buildings and resources. You have to get at the question of equal dignity. Whether that 9–0 decision actually got there depended on what local communities and institutions were willing to do with it.

You get the whole thing from that green light out across the water. It looks close enough to grab, and that's what keeps Gatsby going. The water in between is the part he won't look at. Daisy has changed, and the past is done with. He doesn't care. Money and enough determination will get him back to that girl he remembers. Tell Nick he can repeat the past and you have the whole of him. That dream is the only thing he trusts.

The end in Chapter 8 is the part that makes it a tragedy. Daisy drives the car that kills Myrtle. Then Gatsby sits out on the porch to take the blame. She says nothing. Wilson comes looking for his revenge and puts a bullet into Gatsby in his own pool. She gets away from all of it. He dies alone, still holding on to a dream that was never going to come back.

You have to grant him the same standing as the old tragic heroes. The dream is what made him something, and the same dream is what got him killed. That light he was always reaching for was never going to be a promise. It was just a way to keep on reaching for a future that was out of his reach. You have to admire the hope in that. It got him killed, sure, but it was the only thing he had. The fact that he got his wealth from criminal activity doesn't take that away.

You've got the two biggest pieces already. The nine to nothing vote tells you this wasn't a close call or a matter of party lines. You can find a few of the justices who had voted for segregation in other cases. That they all signed off on this one means the old "separate but equal" idea had run out of legal road. You can't really argue the system was equal when the schools for black kids got less money and worse facilities. The decision just made that inequality impossible to defend in a court of law.

That said the ruling didn't actually get most kids into those schools right away. You'd have to look at the years of "massive resistance" that followed to see the full picture. Southern states closed their own schools rather than mix them. The change you got from the decision was a legal one first and a social one only later. Still that legal shift gave later activists something to work from. They had a ruling from the highest court in the land to back them up. Without that 1954 starting point the whole movement that followed would have had to fight on a much weaker footing.

The case also set a pattern for how the courts would handle other civil rights questions down the line. You see the same kind of reasoning in later fights over voting rights and public accommodations. The nine to nothing vote made all of that possible by knocking out the central legal defense for the old order. That is the part of the story that matters most when you look back. It wasn't the end of the fight but it did take the fight off the old ground.

You get the green light from the first page out. It's Daisy's dock, five miles off, and Gatsby keeps his eyes on it the way a man keeps his eyes on a thing he's already lost. That's your tragedy right there, the whole thing built on a past he can't actually get back. He throws these enormous parties to get her to come over, but the light stays the same distance. You can drive right up to it and you still can't touch it. The light never gets any closer, and that's the whole of his mistake. He mistook a figure in the distance for something he could hold.

It all comes apart in the last chapter. You have Myrtle run out in front of his car, and then Daisy takes the wheel and drives off. Gatsby ends up taking the blame for that, and Wilson ends up taking his gun. He shoots Gatsby in his own pool and then kills himself. Nobody comes to the funeral. The people who had so eagerly eaten at his table have vanished. You're left with the light still burning over the water. It hasn't changed one bit. He had the whole of his life to get to that point and he still failed to reach it.

That last failure is what makes him tragic rather than merely foolish. He had the means to do almost anything, and he spent it all trying to put the clock back. The light was there to show him exactly what he was after, and he never once doubted that he could have it. He just got the facts of the matter wrong. When he dies he has got nothing to show for it, and the thing he wanted most remains forever out of his reach. That is the whole of the story and there is no getting around it.

You want to know if the bob's weight changes how long a swing takes. You don't. The period, meaning the time for one full back and forth trip, came out to about 1.4 seconds for both the 50 g and 200 g bobs. That was with the string held at 0.5 m. You get the same answer from the math. The equation \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}\) has no place for mass in it, and it predicts 1.42 seconds for that length of string. Our 1.4 second result is close enough to back that up.

You are going to pick up a few things you didn't mean to. A person starting and stopping a stopwatch is bound to be off by a bit. You also have to put up with air resistance and some friction at the support. If you let go from too steep an angle the whole thing stops matching the ideal case. You'd have to measure a single swing to get that bad a result though.

You can get around most of that. Time 10 or 20 swings and then divide the total up. Run the whole thing again a few times and take the average. You end up in the same place you were the first time. Keep the string the same length and the mass of the bob won't touch the period.

You set the 50 g bob in motion and it came back to the starting point in 1.4 seconds. You then swapped it for the 200 g one and got the same 1.4 second result. That second run was the one that really mattered, since it showed the first wasn't some fluke. With the string locked at 0.5 m the only thing you were changing was how much the bob weighed. The data you got out of that says weight has no part in setting the clock. You are getting the same period the whole time because the restoring force the earth exerts on the bob grows in exact proportion to the mass you are moving. A heavier bob has more of that force to act on it, and the two effects end up canceling each other out.

That said you did run into a bit of noise in the numbers. Your stopwatch was only accurate to a tenth of a second and a few of your release points were not perfectly vertical. Those small mistakes are enough to explain the last bit of variation you saw. None of that variation followed the change in mass though. If you had kept changing the weight the pattern would have held. You would have to go in and change the length of the string to get a different period out of the whole thing. That is the one variable that actually gets in there and changes the result.

You get a lot of the story wrong if you think the press was just a faster copy machine. Around 1440 Gutenberg got together movable metal type, a certain ink, and a press to crank out identical pages. That got books off the backs of monks and out into a real market. People had to learn to read to get their hands on them. Once they could, the whole setup let ideas jump over borders and the usual social barriers. Scholars finally had enough of the same texts to compare and build on. You see the effect in the way the Renaissance got hold of art, science, and the old Greek and Roman stuff. Copernicus and Vesalius got their observations out that way, and better maps and manuals went to work on trade and navigation.

The same thing happened to religion and the state. Luther put his gripes against the Catholic Church into pamphlets and that got the Protestant Reformation going. Rulers and churches got a new way to push laws and beliefs around. You got propaganda and rumors along with it. With more people able to read, the old authorities found themselves getting questioned. None of this got around to everyone. Women, the poor, and the people out in the country still went without much schooling or books. Rulers also kept a close eye on printers and shut down what they took for rebellion. The whole thing still ended up changing things for good. You got a much faster exchange of knowledge that built up modern science and politics. In the end it just gave ideas a bigger audience to work on.

It starts with the sun beating down on the oceans, lakes, and rivers. That heat gets the water to change from a liquid into a gas called water vapor. You can't see this vapor as it drifts up into the sky. Once it gets high enough the air is much colder, and that cold makes the vapor change back into the tiniest liquid drops. Those drops keep joining together until they form the clouds you see overhead. The clouds keep getting heavier and heavier until the drops can't be held up any longer. That is when they come back down to the earth as rain, sleet, or snow. The water that lands on the ground then trickles into streams and runs back out to the big bodies of water. From there the whole thing gets to start over again. You can see this happening every single day all around you. You just have to look up to see it. The whole thing keeps on going in one long unbroken chain.

You're seeing the whole thing every time you get rained on. The Sun beats down on oceans, lakes, rivers, and the puddle outside your window. That heat turns the liquid into vapor you can't see. It goes up. Up to where it's cold enough for that vapor to cool off. It clings to bits of dust and you get a cloud. The cloud keeps filling up with droplets and ice until it can't hold out. Then the stuff comes down as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. It ends up back in the same places it started, oceans and lakes and rivers, or it gets stored in glaciers and under ground. You get your share from it too. You drink it and so do the animals, and the plants pull it in. The Sun gets at that collected water again and you are off in the same loop. You get fresh water out of the deal and the land gets carved along the way. It also keeps the planet from getting too hot. You wouldn't get very far without it. Nothing would.

You can't get around the fact that everything before 1440 was just too slow. A single Bible took a monk months to copy out by hand, which meant the thing you could get your hands on was the thing your local monastery happened to have on hand. Gutenberg's machine flipped that. You could get a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand copies of the same thing in a matter of weeks. That got ideas moving in a way they never had before. A pamphlet arguing for religious reform in one city would be in the next before the authorities could get their act together. You ended up with a public that had to think for itself since so many different points of view were now available.

That same speed got the new scientific findings out to the people who could use them. A natural philosopher in Italy no longer had to wait a generation for his work to reach England. Everyone was working from the same set of facts instead of the mangled versions that hand copying produced. The old order of things got pretty hard to keep up with once that many people had access to the same information. You got a whole lot of political and social change out of that, none of which would have been possible on the old hand copying system. The whole of Europe ended up looking very different for it. You just have to look at the dates to see how fast that change came.

You get summer in the Northern Hemisphere because the whole planet is leaning in to the Sun. The axis is off by 23.5 degrees and it keeps that same aim no matter where Earth is in its trip around the Sun. Lean in and you get more direct rays and longer days. That is summer up there. The South is leaning out of the way at the same time, so it gets the short days and cold of winter. You are just waiting for the other side of the orbit to get the same thing six months later. The South gets its turn then. Spring and fall are what you get in between, when neither half of the planet has much of an angle to speak of. You might think the part of the trip where Earth is a bit closer to the Sun has something to do with it. It does not. That angle and the hours of daylight you get are the only things that really matter. The whole thing is just that tilted axis going around.

You get the short answer by looking at the Earth's wobble. The planet keeps that 23.5 degree tilt pointed at the same spot in space the whole time it goes around the sun. That fixed angle is the whole trick. When the north end of the axis leans in the sun's direction you get longer days and more direct rays in that part of the world. That is your summer. The other half of the planet is leaning away and has to make do with slanted light and shorter days. You call that winter. Six months later the situation is exactly the other way around. You would not have this whole cycle if the axis stood straight up. In that case every part of the globe would get pretty much the same amount of sun all year long. The changing of the light is what you have come to call the changing of the seasons. None of this has to do with the earth being closer to or farther from the sun. The distance does change a bit but that is far too small a thing to account for the changes you see.

That gets you to about two hundred words and keeps to the one paragraph you were asked for. You might want to read it out loud to see if the flow works for you. The main thing is that you have not gotten the direction of the tilt and the resulting effects mixed up.

You're looking at a pretty clean example of how temperature runs the whole show. The 18 mL of CO2 you got at 35C is the yeast working at close to full capacity. That's right in the middle of the range where the enzymes handling glycolysis and fermentation are most active. You've got fast sugar breakdown, which you see as a lot of gas. Drop the same setup to 15C and the whole thing slows to a crawl. You ended up with 6 mL, which is just one third of the warmer run. That isn't some change in the yeast's basic ability to make gas. The cells are still there and the sugar is still available. You've just made the molecular machinery inside them move much more slowly. You'd probably get the same sort of ratio if you had tried 25C.

The only real danger in the warmer run is that you get close to the point where the enzymes start to break down. Push that 35C much further and you'd be cooking the very things you need. You've clearly avoided that in this case. You can see the whole thing is a fairly direct line from the temperature you set to the amount of gas you got. If you ran the experiment again you'd almost certainly get the same result. The cells at the low temperature aren't any less capable, they are just working on a much slower clock. That 15C environment simply doesn't give them the energy they need to get through the sugar at the rate you saw under the warmer conditions. You got your numbers from that difference in the rate of reaction.

You got 18 mL of CO2 out of the yeast in 20 minutes at 35C. Drop the temperature to 15C and you get 6 mL in the same time. That works out to 0.9 mL a minute against 0.3. The yeast is just three times faster in the warm water. You already know the rest. It chews up glucose, and when the oxygen runs out it goes into fermentation. That process turns the sugar into ethanol and the CO2 you are measuring. The whole thing runs on enzymes. Cranking the temperature up gets the enzyme and substrate particles moving faster. They hit each other more often and more of those hits actually work. You get more gas. The 15C setup is just the same thing with less energy around to get the job done.

That said you have no idea if the rate keeps climbing. Push the heat past the yeast's limit and the enzymes fall apart, and the whole thing grinds to a halt. 35C is probably close to that limit but you would have to test more points to be sure. You are also at the mercy of a bunch of other things. The glucose you used, how much of it there was, the pH, the amount of yeast, and how well you could measure the gas all got to affect the outcome. Running the whole thing a few times at each temperature and taking the mean would sort some of that out. Keep the apparatus, the volumes, and the timing the same every time. A water bath would keep the temperature from wandering, and a quick check for leaks would keep the CO2 numbers from getting too far off. All of that said the numbers you have in hand do back up the idea that a bit of extra heat speeds the process along.

You already know the first half of this. Phones are how you talk to people, get news, and get off on your own ideas. The trouble is what that gets you to do at 2 am. We polled the class and 19 out of 27 of you are out there on those things after midnight. That's not an edge case. It is the norm and it is taking a toll on your health and your grades.

You can't just put the thing down. You mean to look at one message and end up three hours deep in some video or argument. The whole system is built to keep your eyes on the glass, and the hours just slip away. You end up with a lot less sleep than you need. The light pouring out of that glass doesn't help either. It tells your brain the day is still going, particularly if you are up close to when you should be asleep. On top of that you get the jolt of a new message or the heat of some online fight. None of that makes it easy to wind down.

You pay for that lost sleep in the morning. You can't get your head into a class, you can't keep what you do learn, and the homework piles up. You end up irritable and out of it. Keep that up and you are going to wreck your body and your mind. You can back off on all of this by picking a hard stop for the night. Leave the phone out of the bedroom, kill the pings, and get an actual alarm clock. Your school and your family need to get behind that kind of routine.

You are not going to get out of this one without some of that. The survey we ran proves that almost everyone is in the same boat. You will sleep better and do better in school once midnight marks the end of the screen time.

You get a three day weekend. That alone would knock out a lot of the grogginess that comes from getting up early five days in a row. Kids would come back to class actually ready to pay attention. You'd see the same thing on the teacher side. That free day is worth a lot for getting through the lesson planning and grading that piles up. Less burnout usually means a more interesting class to sit in. Families also get a real chance to get to appointments that now force a kid to miss a day of school.

You are going to hear that the shorter week means longer days or less time to learn. That part makes sense. The way to get around it is to stretch out the school day a bit or just use the fifth day for optional tutoring, clubs and meals. You'd also have to set up some kind of childcare for the families that depend on it. None of that is impossible to put in place.

If you get the details right the whole thing works out. You end up with less stress and more time for the family. Kids are going to learn more when they are healthy and actually have time to get some rest. That is the whole of the case for trying it.

You'd think cutting a day would just mean less learning, but the math doesn't work out that way. Right now most of us are so burned out by the end of Friday that we can't absorb anything anyway. Give that time back and you get kids who are actually ready to pay attention. You can fit the same amount of material into four longer days if you stop padding the schedule with busy work. The extra weekend day isn't so much a vacation as it is a chance to get that busy work done on your own. Plenty of districts that have tried this are already seeing better test scores, not worse ones. The only thing that seems to suffer is the old habit of showing up to a building for the sake of it.

That said you are going to run into a lot of parents who can't get together for child care. That is a real problem and it doesn't get solved by a new calendar. You'd have to build in some kind of after school support to keep it from just shuffling the same old troubles into a different day. If you can get that part right though the whole thing works out. You end up with a schedule that gives you more time to actually think.

You already have the best part of this done. That 19 out of 27 number is your whole first paragraph. You can say that in our own class the pattern is obvious, and then you don't have to waste space on generalities. The phones are the problem, and the problem is the blue light they throw off. That light tricks the brain into thinking it is still daytime, so the body stops making the melatonin it needs to get to sleep. You end up in a loop where you are too wired to rest, and the next day you are running on a short fuse.

The damage isn't just that you are getting less of it. You are also missing the deep stages of rest that your brain needs to sort out the day. That is why the kid who stayed up to the third act of a video game ends up in a fog all the next day. The habit gets worse because the apps are built to keep you looking at them. Every like and comment gives a little hit of the same thing your brain gets from food or drugs. You get hooked on the next thing that is going to happen, and the clock keeps running behind.

You can get out of it, but you have to take the phone out of the room. Keeping it on your person is just an invitation to give in to the next notification. If you put it in a drawer in the next room the habit starts to die. It will take a little while for your body to get back to a normal schedule, but that is the only way to get it. The class survey you have in hand proves that this is a shared problem, and a shared solution is the only one that is going to work.

You can't live on $7.25. That's been the federal minimum wage since 2009. Work 40 hours a week at that rate and you end up with roughly $15,000 a year before the government takes its cut. That doesn't cover rent, food, getting around, or health care in most of the country. You end up in poverty or stuck on public assistance. Bumping the wage to $15 gets a lot of people out of that hole.

You'll hear that small businesses can't take the hit. They'll have to jack up prices, cut hours, or let people go. That risk is real in places where the cost of living is low. You also get something out of it. People who are paid more stick around, and you stop bleeding money on constant hiring and training. All that extra cash gets spent back into the local economy. You can get around the one size fits all problem by rolling the thing out in stages or letting local rules fill in the gaps. The feds still need to set that floor though. Nobody working full time should be unable to get by.

It won't fix the whole economy. It will put more money in the hands of the people who are doing the work. That's a pretty good place to start.

You can't get a decent life on what the current minimum pays. Thirteen dollars an hour in 2014 got you by. You can't do that in 2024. A fifteen dollar floor doesn't hand out handouts so much as it stops employers from paying people less than the cost of the work they do. You see the same thing in the states that already got there. Washington, Oregon, and California all raised the number and kept their local economies going. The small panic that gets talked up in the papers never materialized.

That said the whole thing falls apart if you try to apply it to a small town in the middle of nowhere. A five and dime in rural Mississippi can't keep its doors open on the same terms as a chain in Seattle. The result ends up being a lot of people getting laid off instead of getting a raise. You'd be better off with a system that scales the number to match the local cost of living. That gets you the same result without forcing a one size fits all rule on everybody.

The people who keep insisting that any kind of increase will wreck the place are mostly just afraid of paying more. They have the numbers to back up their claims. What they don't have is any experience with the way these things actually work out once they get into the field. You end up with a more stable group of workers who can actually keep the place running. That is something the current setup has never been able to provide. Getting to that point requires you to set a number that reflects the work being done.

You get the idea from the way your body handles a real infection, only you get it in a much safer form. A vaccine is mostly made up of antigens, which are the parts of a germ your defenses key on. You get a dead version of the germ, a harmless piece of it, or a set of instructions for your own cells to make that piece. The first time you meet an antigen your B cells have to figure out what to do. They start out by making a slow and somewhat clumsy batch of antibodies. That first response is too late to matter much, which is why you might get a mild version of the disease.

The part that actually pays off is what happens next. A number of the B cells that took part in that first response turn into memory cells. These cells hang around for years, or in some cases for the rest of your life, keeping a very specific record of the antigen they met. You are now in a state of readiness. If the real thing shows up later the memory cells spring into action at once. They pour out the right kind of antibodies in such a short time that the germ never gets a chance to get you sick. The whole thing is a bit of a training run that leaves your defenses far better prepared for the real fight.

You might find yourself getting a second or third dose to get the most out of the process. Each of these encounters gives the memory cell population a chance to grow and to get more accurate. That is why the protection you end up with is so much more reliable than the body's first, somewhat haphazard attempt to get the job done.

You'd be doing your neighbors a favor by putting twelve turbines up. That's enough to power 9,000 homes and get us off coal, oil, and gas. Nobody gets a free ride out of that switch, but you end up with cleaner air. That matters a lot for kids and the elderly. Fossil fuels are going to run out anyway. Relying on the wind keeps the local supply from getting so tied to the next fuel price spike.

The money side works out too. You get a round of construction jobs right off the bat, and the town ends up with extra tax revenue to put toward schools and roads. You still need people to keep the whole thing running once it's up. A few of those people might end up showing the place to visitors. The land around the blades doesn't have to go to waste either. You can keep it in for farming or grazing.

You're going to hear the usual gripes about the noise, the looks, and the birds. That's only fair. You can back the machines off from the houses, and the newer models are a lot quieter. Getting in some experts to keep an eye on the wildlife is a given. The town has to put down some real safety rules and let people have a say before the first shovel hits the ground. That's as far as you should go to hold this up. You ought to get it done.

You get the same training out of a vaccine that you would from a real infection, minus the damage. The shot gets some form of the virus or bacterium into your body. That form might be a weakened or killed version of the whole thing, or just a protein, a bit of genetic instruction, or some other harmless part. You'll see these bits called antigens. Your immune cells take one look and flag them as foreign. That flag sets the whole response in motion. You get a bunch of B cells that end up as plasma cells, and those plasma cells pump out antibodies. The antibodies grab onto the pathogen's antigens, either to stop it in its tracks or to tag it for destruction.

That first round also leaves behind a few memory B cells. They stick around long after the vaccine is gone, and they know exactly what to do. If the real pathogen shows up later, those cells hit back faster and harder. You end up with memory T cells in the mix too, and those help out by either calling in the rest of the response or taking out infected cells. The whole thing usually gets the pathogen killed off before it has a chance to get you sick. You'll need some of these shots more than once. The extra doses keep the response strong, and they make up for the fact that antibody levels and memory cell numbers drop off with time. You are still going to catch some of these things. What you won't get is the worst of the illness, and the odds of you passing it on go way down.

That last part is what keeps the rest of the group safe. Get enough people in the community immune and the pathogen runs out of places to go. That in turn looks after the people who can't get the shots. You've just taken a first encounter with an antigen and made it into a defense that is both quicker and more effective.

You are saving trees, water, and energy every time you put a can, bottle, or cardboard box in the right bin. You are also keeping that stuff out of the landfills. The factories that would have made all that new stuff from raw materials end up making less, which means less pollution. You saw this work at our own school. We got 1.2 tons of paper out of the trash last year. That number got the whole student and teacher body working together. You can get in on that by reusing your old notebooks and skipping the products wrapped in ten layers of plastic. You are not going to fix the whole thing with recycling alone though. You have to buy less and get more out of what you already have. That said, the daily choices you make do add up to cleaner neighborhoods and better air. You will be setting the terms for the people who come after you. That is true for the kids in your class just as much as for anyone else.

You are going to have to skip the part about how your choices shape tomorrow. You already know that. The 1.2 tons of paper is the only proof you need that the whole thing works.

You've probably got a stack of old tests and worksheets in your locker right now. That pile would have ended up in a landfill if the paper collection bins in the hallways hadn't been there. Last year the whole school managed to pull 1.2 tons of paper out of that waste stream. You might not see what that number means until you picture the trees that got to stay standing. Those trees would otherwise have been cut down to make new sheets. You also get to keep the water and energy that the paper mills would have used. That is a lot of water to save when you are only talking about one school year. The whole thing works out to a pretty nice result for the neighborhood. You are getting the same clean sheets to write on without paying that hidden cost in the way of destroyed forests. It is not exactly a grand gesture to drop a used sheet into a bin, but the bins only work if you keep using them. The 1.2 tons you helped to collect proves that the whole thing is more than just a good idea. It is something that actually gets done.

You can't get around the math. Twelve turbines will keep the lights on in 9,000 houses, and that's a lot of coal you're not burning. You've probably got a coal plant somewhere downwind already, and that's what you're actually breathing. Swapping that out for something that just makes a low rumble is a pretty good trade. The noise is the sort of thing your ears get used to in a day or two. You stop noticing it the way you've stopped noticing the hum of the highway. The coal smoke has no such habit of getting out of your system.

That said you'd be hard put to find a site that doesn't anger somebody. You'd be trading a health hazard for a visual one. Nobody in town is going to get rich off the deal either. The money mostly ends up in the pockets of the people who own the equipment. You'd just be getting the benefit of cleaner air for your trouble. That benefit is worth a lot more than the view you'd be giving up. You've got to weigh what you can't see against what you can. The air you get back is something you can't buy any other way.

The project isn't going to be perfect. You'll get some complaints about the way the blades catch the light. You'll have to live with a few of the things you don't like. You've been living with far worse things for a long time now. Getting the coal out of the picture is the only part of that that really matters. Everything else is just a matter of getting used to it.

You see them suit up in a hurry. That gear is heavy, the helmets and breathing rigs included, and they don't wait around to get it on. They go right in. You get families out, and the pets, and plenty of people they've never met. You get car wrecks and the occasional flood to deal with as well. It isn't just a matter of being brave either. You need the training, the patience, and the whole group working together. They keep their heads while they follow a plan that's already been thought through. That same group gets out to show folks how to check smoke alarms and get an escape route in order. I'd want to ask them what all that work is like if I ever got the chance. You don't see any special powers in it. Just a lot of hard work and some pretty plain old kindness. I figure that's the sort of thing I ought to be doing for my own neighborhood.

The part about true heroes not needing powers is a little much, though. That sort of thing gets you in trouble with the people who actually do the work. They aren't out there trying to make a point about what heroism looks like. They are just trying to get people out of a bad fix. You can't get much further from the idea of some kind of superman. The work is too much of a daily grind to be dressed up in that fashion.

My favorite person in the neighborhood is Mrs. Gable, who has run the little corner library for twenty years. You can always find her behind the front desk, but that is only the tip of what she does. She has a way of getting the most reluctant readers to open a book. Last spring she set up a whole series of story hours for the kids who had been shut out of the school programs. That got a group of fifth graders to start a reading club that still meets every Saturday. Nobody else in the area seems to have that kind of patience or interest in what the kids are getting out of the books. I have never seen anyone else try so hard to get a whole group of people to enjoy something. You could call that kind of work a little thing, but it has changed the way the whole neighborhood gets together. That sort of quiet, steady help is what I find most admirable.
