**A $15 Federal Minimum Wage Is Overdue**

The federal minimum wage has sat at $7.25 since 2009. In those fifteen years, consumer prices have climbed more than 40 percent, meaning the lowest-paid American workers have quietly taken a steep pay cut. A full-time minimum-wage job now pays about $15,000 a year — below the poverty line for a parent with one child. Congress should raise the floor to $15 an hour, phased in over several years and indexed to inflation thereafter.

First, $15 is less a raise than a restoration. The minimum wage reached its peak real value in 1968, when it was worth roughly $13 in today's dollars. Had it kept pace with worker productivity since then, it would be far higher than $15. Asking for $15 is not a radical demand; it is catching up to a standard America already met half a century ago.

Second, a higher wage floor reduces poverty and cuts public costs. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that a $15 wage would lift roughly 900,000 people out of poverty. Right now, taxpayers subsidize low-wage employers: when companies pay wages that cannot cover rent or groceries, workers turn to Medicaid and food assistance to survive. Decent pay shifts that burden back to the businesses profiting from the labor.

Critics argue that jobs would disappear, and the CBO did project employment losses. But a growing body of research — notably Cengiz and colleagues' study of 138 state minimum-wage increases — finds that higher minimums raise earnings at the bottom without meaningfully reducing the number of low-wage jobs. Employers offset costs through lower turnover, higher productivity, and modest price increases. Cities and states that already exceed $15 have not collapsed.

The strongest objection is regional: $15 bites harder in rural Mississippi than in Seattle. That is an argument for a gradual phase-in, not for freezing the wage at poverty levels indefinitely.

Vaccines train the immune system to recognize and fight a pathogen, such as a virus or bacterium, before a person encounters it naturally. They expose the body to harmless forms or parts of the pathogen, or instructions for making one of its proteins. This prepares the immune system without causing the disease that the vaccine is designed to prevent.

The key targets in this process are antigens: molecules that the immune system recognizes as foreign. After vaccination, immune cells take up vaccine material and display pieces of its antigens. This helps activate helper T cells, which coordinate the immune response. B cells whose receptors match the antigen can also become activated, often with help from these T cells.

Activated B cells multiply and develop into plasma cells or memory B cells. Plasma cells produce antibodies, which are proteins that bind specifically to the antigen. Antibodies can block a virus from entering cells or mark pathogens for destruction by other immune cells. Some vaccines also stimulate killer T cells, which destroy infected body cells.

Once the initial response ends, many activated immune cells disappear. However, memory cells, including memory B cells and memory T cells, remain. Some plasma cells also survive and continue producing antibodies. If the real pathogen later enters the body, memory cells recognize its antigens and respond more quickly and strongly. This can prevent illness or reduce its severity.

Protection is not always immediate or lifelong. The immune system needs time to build its response, and immunity may weaken over time. Booster doses remind the immune system of the antigen and strengthen its defenses. Although vaccines do not guarantee complete protection, they greatly reduce the risk of many serious infections. By reducing infections and, for some diseases, transmission, vaccination can also help protect vulnerable people in the community.

The Pythagorean theorem, expressed as $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, reveals a fundamental geometric relationship in right-angled triangles. It states that the square of the hypotenuse (the longest side, opposite the right angle) is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides. This principle works because it represents a conservation of area. If you construct a square on each side of a right triangle, the area of the square on the hypotenuse is exactly equal to the combined areas of the squares on the two legs.

To visualize this, consider the classic 3-4-5 triangle. The two shorter sides (legs) measure 3 units and 4 units, while the hypotenuse measures 5 units. First, we calculate the area of the square built on the side of length 3, which is $3^2 = 9$. Next, we calculate the area of the square on the side of length 4, which is $4^2 = 16$. When we add these two areas together ($9 + 16$), we get a total of 25.

Now, look at the square built on the hypotenuse of length 5. Its area is $5^2$, which also equals 25. This numerical equality is not a coincidence; it is a geometric necessity. The theorem works because the geometric shape of the right triangle forces the areas to balance in this specific way. Whether you use physical tiles, algebraic proofs, or geometric dissections, the 3-4-5 triangle consistently demonstrates that the "space" contained in the hypotenuse’s square is perfectly filled by the combined "space" of the leg squares. This universal truth allows us to calculate unknown distances in navigation, construction, and physics with precision.

**Finding the Area of a Circle with Radius 4 cm**

To find the area of a circle, use the formula **A = πr²**, where *r* is the radius. Here, the radius is 4 cm, so first square the radius: 4 × 4 = 16. Then multiply by pi: 16 × 3.14 = **50.24 cm²**. (Using the π button on a calculator gives about 50.27 cm².) Remember that area is always measured in square units, so the answer is in square centimeters.

We use pi because every circle, no matter its size, has the same ratio between its circumference and its diameter. That ratio is pi, approximately 3.14. Since circles curve instead of having straight sides, we can't just multiply length by width like a rectangle. Pi connects a circle's straight measurement (the radius) to its curved shape. If you imagine slicing a circle into thin wedges and rearranging them, they form a rectangle-like shape whose area equals πr².

**Statistics Project Explanation: Time Spent on Homework**

For our Grade 11 statistics project, our group investigated the question: *How much time do students at our school spend on homework each night?* We chose this topic because homework load is something every student has an opinion about, but we wanted actual data rather than assumptions.

We collected data by surveying 60 students using a short questionnaire that asked how many minutes they spent on homework the previous school night. To reduce bias, we distributed the survey across several different classes and grade levels rather than only asking our friends, who likely have study habits similar to our own. Our sample of 60 was large enough to show a clear pattern but small enough to collect and organize within our deadline.

After recording the responses, we ordered the data from least to greatest and found the median time was **75 minutes**. The median is the middle value, so with 60 responses we averaged the 30th and 31st values. We deliberately reported the median instead of the mean because our data contained several outliers—a few students reported spending over four hours on homework, which would have pulled the mean upward and made the typical experience look heavier than it really is. The median resists this distortion, so it describes the "typical" student more honestly.

Our conclusion is that a typical student at our school spends about an hour and a quarter on homework nightly. However, our results have limitations: the sample was not randomly selected, students self-reported their times from memory, and homework loads vary by night and by course selection.

### How Social Media Affects Teenagers’ Sleep

Social media is a major part of teenage life, offering entertainment, friendship, and a way to stay connected. However, it can also interfere with sleep. In our class survey, 19 of 27 students reported using their phones after midnight. This is about 70 percent of the class, suggesting that late phone use is common among the students we surveyed.

One reason social media affects sleep is that it makes bedtime easy to postpone. Short videos, messages, and endless feeds encourage users to keep scrolling. A teenager who plans to check one notification may spend another hour online. Screen light can also delay the body’s preparation for sleep, while exciting or upsetting content may make it harder to relax.

Losing sleep can affect teenagers the next day. They may struggle to concentrate, remember information, or participate in lessons. Tiredness can also increase irritability and make everyday stress harder to manage. Since teenagers generally need eight to ten hours of sleep each night, regularly staying awake past midnight can be especially problematic when school starts early.

However, our survey has limitations. It involved only 27 students, and phone use does not necessarily mean social media use. It also did not measure sleep length or quality. Therefore, it cannot prove that social media caused sleep problems or represent all teenagers. Still, the result provides a useful starting point for discussing bedtime habits.

Social media is not entirely harmful because it can help teenagers maintain friendships and find support. The goal should be balance rather than a complete ban. Turning off notifications, setting an evening limit, and charging phones away from the bed can reduce distractions. Families and schools can encourage these habits without blaming teenagers. By protecting sleep, young people can enjoy social media while giving their health and learning the attention they deserve.

Gutenberg’s system of movable metal type made it possible to produce many copies much faster and at a lower cost.

As books became more affordable, more people could read and learn. Printed textbooks helped education expand, while books in local languages, rather than only Latin, reached wider audiences. Literacy grew gradually, and knowledge became less dependent on access to rare handwritten manuscripts.

The printing press also helped spread Renaissance ideas. Works by ancient Greek and Roman writers became more widely available. Scholars could compare texts and share new arguments. Later, scientists used printed books and diagrams to communicate discoveries, allowing others to test and build upon their work.

Printing also transformed religion. In the early 1500s, Martin Luther’s writings spread rapidly through printed pamphlets. These publications helped the Protestant Reformation gain support and challenged the authority of the Catholic Church. Printed Bible translations allowed more readers to study religious texts themselves.

The effects were not only positive. Printing could spread false information and hostile propaganda as easily as useful knowledge. Governments and religious authorities sometimes censored books because they feared challenges to their power. Overall, Gutenberg’s press changed Europe by making information easier to reproduce and distribute. It did not transform society overnight, but it helped reshape education, religion, science, and public debate for centuries to come.

**Should the Voting Age Be Lowered to 16?**

Democracy rests on a simple principle: people affected by the law should have a say in who makes it. Sixteen-year-olds already feel that effect. Many work and pay taxes, all are shaped by decisions about schools, climate policy, and public transport, and in many countries they can leave education or consent to medical treatment. Yet they have no vote. Lowering the voting age to 16 would close that gap.

The strongest argument is practical rather than theoretical, because the experiment has already been run. In 2007, Austria became the first country in the European Union to lower the voting age to 16 for all elections. The results contradicted the pessimists. Researchers found that Austrian 16- and 17-year-olds turned out at rates comparable to older first-time voters, and that the choices they made matched their own stated political preferences about as closely as adults' choices did. In other words, they voted competently.

There is also a case about habit. Voting is learned behaviour, and people who vote in their first eligible election tend to keep voting. At 16, most teenagers are still in school, living at home, and able to discuss politics in civics lessons. At 18, many are moving house, starting work, or beginning university, which makes registration and participation harder.

Critics argue that 16-year-olds lack maturity. But maturity varies enormously at every age, and we do not test adults for political knowledge before letting them vote. Rights should not depend on passing an informal competence exam.

Extending the franchise to 16 would strengthen democracy, not weaken it.

---

**Title: Analyzing Academic Burden: A Statistical Study on Homework Duration**

In our Grade 11 mathematics unit, we conducted a statistical survey to analyze the typical time students dedicate to daily homework. The primary objective was to determine a representative measure of central tendency for our peer group’s academic workload. We selected a sample size of 60 students from various classes to ensure a diverse and relatively balanced representation of the school population. The data collected focused specifically on the average number of minutes spent on homework per day.

To process the data, we first organized the 60 data points in ascending order. Since our sample size is even, the median was calculated by averaging the two middle values, which were the 30th and 31st data points. This calculation revealed that the median time spent on homework was exactly 75 minutes. The median was chosen as our primary metric because it is robust against outliers; unlike the mean, it is not skewed by extreme values, such as students who spend significantly less or more time on assignments. For instance, if a few students reported zero minutes while others reported four hours, the mean would be distorted, but the median would remain a reliable indicator of the "typical" student’s experience.

The finding of a 75-minute median suggests that the central tendency of our peer group’s homework load is moderate. This data point provides a baseline for comparing academic demands across different subjects or grade levels. Furthermore, this project highlighted the importance of sampling methods and data interpretation. By analyzing the distribution, we observed that while 75 minutes is the median, the range of times varied significantly, indicating that individual experiences differ widely.

In conclusion, this project demonstrated how statistical tools like the median can provide clear insights into student life. The 75-minute median serves as a crucial benchmark, helping educators and students alike understand the average academic time commitment required for high school success.

I solved this problem by separating the fixed cost of the phone plan from the cost of the text messages. The fixed cost is $25, which means that amount is charged no matter how many texts are sent. Each text message adds $0.10 to the bill.

Next, I needed to find how many texts would cost $12. Since each text costs $0.10, I divided $12 by $0.10. The result was 120, so **120 text messages** were sent. Another way to think about this is that one dollar pays for ten texts, so twelve dollars pays for 120 texts.

**Why the Pythagorean Theorem Works**

The theorem says that in a right triangle, the squares on the two legs together equal the square on the hypotenuse. For a 3-4-5 triangle: 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5².

Here is why this must happen. Take four identical copies of the 3-4-5 triangle and place them inside a large square whose side is 3 + 4 = 7, putting one triangle in each corner so that each leg of 3 lines up with a leg of 4. The big square has area 7² = 49. Each triangle has area ½(3)(4) = 6, so the four together cover 24.

The uncovered space in the middle is a tilted quadrilateral. Each of its sides is a hypotenuse, so all four sides measure 5. Its corners are right angles, because at every point the two acute angles of a triangle (which add to 90°) sit on either side of the corner along a straight line of 180°. So the middle shape is a square of side 5.

Therefore its area is 49 − 24 = 25, which means 5² = 25. Since this works for any legs *a* and *b*, we get (a + b)² − 4(½ab) = a² + b² = c².

Our statistics project investigated how much time students spend on homework. We surveyed 60 students and used their responses to identify a typical homework time. The main result was a median of 75 minutes, or one hour and fifteen minutes.

To find the median, we would arrange all 60 reported times from shortest to longest. Because there is an even number of responses, the median is the average of the 30th and 31st values. In our survey, that average was 75 minutes. This means at least half of the reported times were 75 minutes or less, and at least half were 75 minutes or more.

The median is useful because it is less affected by unusually high or low values than the mean. Additionally, surveying 60 students does not automatically make the results representative of the whole school. That depends on how participants were selected.

Overall, our project found that 75 minutes was the middle homework time among the students surveyed. A future study could use a random sample and ask students to record homework time over several days for more reliable results.

The results show that yeast produced more carbon dioxide at 35°C than at 15°C during the same period of 20 minutes. At 35°C, 18 mL of CO₂ was collected, compared with only 6 mL at 15°C. This corresponds to average production rates of 0.9 mL/min and 0.3 mL/min, respectively. Therefore, carbon dioxide production was three times faster at the higher temperature.

This difference can be explained by the effect of temperature on enzyme activity. Yeast breaks down sugars through metabolic reactions controlled by enzymes. At 35°C, molecules generally have more kinetic energy than at 15°C, increasing the frequency of successful collisions between enzymes and substrates. Consequently, these reactions can occur more rapidly. The lower temperature slows metabolism but does not necessarily kill the yeast. If oxygen was limited, the carbon dioxide would mainly result from alcoholic fermentation, which also produces ethanol.

However, these results do not establish that 35°C is the optimum temperature for yeast activity. Only two temperatures were tested, so additional measurements at intermediate and higher temperatures would be needed. At sufficiently high temperatures, enzymes may denature and yeast cells may become damaged, reducing carbon dioxide production.

For a valid comparison, the amount and type of yeast, sugar concentration, solution volume, pH, and incubation time should be kept constant. Possible sources of error include gas leaks, inaccurate volume readings, and temperature fluctuations. Carbon dioxide dissolving in the liquid could also affect the volume collected, especially because gas solubility changes with temperature.

Repeating each treatment several times and calculating mean values would improve reliability. Testing more temperatures would reveal the relationship more clearly. Overall, the data support the conclusion that yeast activity was greater at 35°C under the conditions tested, although the absence of information about repeats and measurement uncertainty limits confidence in the size of the temperature effect.

To find the area of a circle with a radius of 4 cm, use the formula A=πr². Here, A means area, r means radius, and π (pi) is approximately 3.14. The radius is the distance from the center of the circle to its edge.

First, square the radius by multiplying it by itself: 4×4=16. Next, multiply this result by pi: A=16π. Using 3.14 for pi gives 16×3.14=50.24. Therefore, the circle’s area is approximately 50.24 square centimeters. We use square centimeters because area measures the amount of surface inside a shape.

We use pi because it describes a special relationship in every circle: the circumference divided by the diameter always equals pi. If a circle is cut into many thin wedges and rearranged, these pieces nearly form a rectangle with height r and base πr. Its area is therefore πr×r, or πr². Pi connects a circle’s curved boundary to its area.

**Sample Essay (252 words)**

For six weeks, my left hand lived inside a plaster shell. When the cast finally came off, my wrist looked like it belonged to someone else — pale, thin, stiff as a hinge that had rusted shut. The doctor said I'd regain full motion. He didn't mention that my fingers had forgotten how to be a hand.

I had been playing guitar for two years before I fell off my bike. The day after the cast came off, I pulled my guitar out of its case, sat on my bed, and tried to play a G chord. My ring finger wouldn't reach. My wrist wouldn't bend far enough to clear the fretboard. I got through four bars of a song I had once played without thinking, then put the guitar back in the case and didn't open it for a week.

What eventually got me playing again wasn't determination. It was arithmetic. My physical therapist gave me exercises: fifteen repetitions, three times daily. Tedious, measurable, undramatic. I started treating the guitar the same way — not "play the song," but "move this one finger one fret, forty times." Progress came in increments too small to feel, which meant I had to trust the count instead of the feeling.

Eight months later, I played that same song at my school's spring showcase. It wasn't flawless. But I've stopped believing that effort should feel like inspiration. Most of what I've built since — in chemistry, in my work tutoring middle schoolers — has come fifteen repetitions at a time.

**Why this works, so you can replicate it:**

- **Opens mid-scene**, not with a thesis statement ("I have always loved music").
- **Specific sensory details** (plaster, four bars, a G chord) instead of general claims about hardship.
- **Admits failure honestly** — the week of not touching the guitar makes the recovery believable.
- **The insight is modest and surprising.** "It was arithmetic, not determination" is more interesting than "I never gave up."
- **Ends by connecting outward** to other parts of the writer's life, briefly — not with a grand life lesson.

**Scrolling Past Midnight: Social Media and Teenage Sleep**

Doctors recommend that teenagers get eight to ten hours of sleep a night, yet very few of us manage it. The reason is usually not insomnia but choice: we would rather scroll than sleep.

Social media steals sleep in three ways. The first is simple displacement — every minute spent watching short videos is a minute not spent in bed. The second is biological: the blue light from screens suppresses melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel drowsy, so the brain stays alert even after the phone is switched off. The third is psychological. An unresolved group-chat argument, a buzzing notification, or the fear of missing something keeps the mind racing in the dark.

A survey in our own class shows how common the habit is. Of 27 students, 19 — about 70 percent — reported using their phones after midnight. For anyone who has to be awake before seven, that means losing an hour or more of sleep most nights, a debt that piles up until Friday.

The consequences go beyond feeling tired. Sleep is when the brain consolidates memory, so a late night of "studying" with a phone nearby can undo the very learning it was meant to achieve. Research links short sleep in adolescents to poor concentration, lower grades, irritability, weaker immunity, and higher rates of anxiety and depression. Ironically, most of us scroll in order to relax, yet the habit leaves us more stressed the following day.

Fixing this does not require deleting every app. Charging the phone outside the bedroom removes the temptation to check it; an alarm set for bedtime works as well as one set for morning; and if a group of friends agrees on a cut-off time, nobody feels left out. Small changes protect the hours that decide how the whole next day feels.

*(≈310 words)*

**Evidence for "yes, it was right"**
- Slim's judgment carries weight: *"You hadda, George. I swear you hadda."*
- The alternatives were worse — Curley's mob wanted to shoot Lennie "in the guts," and Lennie would otherwise be caged in an institution, which he wouldn't understand.

**Evidence for "no, or at least not simply right"**
- He kills the one person who kept him from the loneliness every other character suffers.
- He never tries to run, hide Lennie, or explain the accident — the killing of Curley's wife *was* an accident.
- He takes a decision that wasn't his to make, however kindly.
- The dream dies with Lennie, and George becomes exactly what he feared: a man alone with his fifty bucks.

**Sentence starters, if you're stuck**
- "What unsettled me most about the ending was…"
- "I think George's choice was less a choice than…"
- "Steinbeck makes it hard to condemn George because…"

One tip: the strongest reflections avoid "it was right" or "it was wrong" flat out, and say something like "it was the kindest option available in a world that offered him no good ones." Pick the version you actually believe, though — that's what makes it sound like you.

The Pythagorean theorem states that, in a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle.

To see why this works, imagine four identical right triangles with legs of lengths a and b and hypotenuse c. Arrange them inside a large square whose sides measure a plus b, placing one triangle at each corner. Their hypotenuses form a smaller, tilted square in the middle. The Greasers are always getting into trouble with the Socs, wealthy teenagers from the other side of town. Ponyboy feels different from the rest of his gang. He reads. The phrase “Stay gold” comes from Robert Frost’s poem “Nothing Gold Can Stay.” Johnny meant it as a warning to Ponyboy to remain kind, hopeful, and true to himself in a world that can be cruel. Gold stood for innocence, beauty, and goodness, things that usually get lost as people grow older. Johnny wanted him to keep that compassion.

The book is powerful because the characters are realistic and the conflicts are still relevant. You should not size a person up from the group he belongs to. The Greasers and the Socs carry the same set of problems, fears, and dreams. Ponyboy learns that empathy can get people to come together. Hinton has made a novel that is sad and inspiring.

You got your insulae for the masses and the domus for the rich. You got up early to pick up bread, vegetables, fruit, or fish in the markets. Kids from the better off families were learning reading, writing, and mathematics. The rest of them picked up their skills at home. The Colosseum opened in 80 AD and it was big enough to hold gladiators, great animal hunts, and other performances. The crowds got pretty loud even when the shows got violent. You could get out of that at the public baths where you washed, exercised, and met up with friends. They had hot, warm, and cold rooms and some of them even had gardens or libraries. You also had to find time to pray to the various gods at the temples and to hear some plays, music, and storytelling. The heat would shut the shops down around noon. That was when you got a bite to eat from bread, olives, cheese, and beans. The streets got going again in the evening. A few homes had lamps to light the way, but the rest of the streets were dark and unsafe. You got a lot of difference between the rich and the poor. That did not stop the whole thing from turning out to be a community built on family, work, religion, and entertainment. You had to put up with the hard parts to get to the baths, markets, and grand buildings.

After World War I the powers signed the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. It helped bring on World War II by leaving Germany angry, with its economy broken, and unable to hold its government together. It was not the only cause. The harsh terms did make it easier for Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party to get support.

Article 231, which was often called the “war guilt clause,” put the blame for the first war on Germany and its allies. That was not what many Germans accepted. They saw the causes as more tangled. The nation had to take the blame all the same, and the democratic government that had agreed to it lost the people's confidence. The whole thing also stung as a national humiliation.

The money terms hit harder. Enormous war reparations went to the victorious countries. That load helped drive the German economy into debt, unemployment, and inflation. In 1923 the government printed huge amounts of money. Hyperinflation followed. Savings went to almost nothing, and many families lost their financial security. Other things also hurt, but the payments stood out as proof that the treaty had been unfair.

Germany also lost territory, military strength, and resources. The army had to be kept small. There could be no air force or submarines. A lot of people took that for being surrounded and dishonored. Adolf Hitler offered to reject the Treaty of Versailles, get the military back on its feet, and put German pride in order. That message found ready listeners among the angry and the desperate.

The clause and the payments bred resentment, and the rest of the restrictions fed German nationalism. That is how the treaty helped set the stage for the next war. Still, the rise of Hitler, the worldwide Great Depression, and the weakness of other countries' responses all had their part.

In Act 2, Scene 1 of *Macbeth* the dagger soliloquy shows a mind that is fearful and more and more violent. He is alone. He asks, “Is this a dagger which I see before me?” He cannot say what he has. The thing may be supernatural, or it may be a hallucination built by his own ambition. He wants the murder and is sick to his teeth with it. It gets into his head until he is obsessed. He reaches for it, “Come, let me clutch thee,” and finds only an image. That difference between what he sees and what he can touch emphasises the trouble in his mind. It seems to lead him on, and in that way stands for the murder and his loss of control. To call it a “fatal vision” is to put death and destiny in one word. He has chosen this future and now finds he cannot get out of it.

Blood does the rest. The blade is covered with “gouts of blood” that are not there, and the real blade will soon be so. That is Duncan's murder coming on, and it shows his thoughts already fouled by violence. The dark place, with its talk of night and witchcraft, makes things threatening. Natural and supernatural forces seem to be joining against him. He knows all the same that his “heat-oppressed brain” made the vision. His last statements are short and decisive. “I go, and it is done” is the sound of a man whose hesitation has turned to determination. The whole thing catches the point at which ambition gets the better of conscience. Shakespeare gets the audience to be sorry for the fear in it, and at the same time shows how imagination, temptation and unchecked ambition push a person toward terrible actions.

The first 500 mL sample of plain water came to a boil at approximately 100°C. That is what you get under normal conditions. The other 500 mL sample got two tablespoons of salt. We stirred it in and then put the heat on. It would not boil until the thermometer showed about 101°C. That is an increase of approximately 1°C. The dissolved salt gets in the way of the water molecules trying to get into the air. The water has to get a little hotter to boil. That is what we had guessed.

We might have read the thermometer wrong, or the salt may not have been measured out exactly. The two samples may not have had exactly the same heating conditions. Some of the salt may have been left undissolved. The change was only a degree, but it was there.

The court got around to the whole thing on May 17, 1954. They all signed on, 9 to 0. That vote took the 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson decision off the books. Plessy had been the thing that let separate but equal facilities get by. Now the court was saying that segregated public schools ran afoul of the Fourteenth Amendment Equal Protection Clause. The whole fight had been going on over what that kind of arrangement did to Black children. Thurgood Marshall and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund kept pointing to the real educational and psychological harm it caused. You could match the buildings and still leave the students marked as inferior. Chief Justice Earl Warren put that in writing by calling separate educational facilities inherently unequal.

You probably could not have gotten that kind of hold on the states with a divided group of justices. They would have found some way to ignore it. The fact that the whole court was in line made it much harder to get around. That same backing helped get the Montgomery Bus Boycott and the later drives for voting rights and public accommodations off the ground. Getting the actual schools to change was a different story. White officials put up enough of a fight to keep some of them apart for years. The 1955 Brown II order to move with all deliberate speed was no help in that regard. The legal direction of the country had still been changed. You now had a settled idea that equality meant more than just identical resources. That sort of thing is still up to the local communities and their institutions to get done.

The ancient Egyptians made the pyramids mainly as tombs for the pharaohs, or kings. They were sure that life continued after death, and that made a safe place for the body and the belongings a necessity. Food, clothing, jewelry, furniture, and sometimes a boat went in with the pharaoh for the journey to the afterlife. The pointed shape may have been the rays of the sun, to lift the king to the sky and let him join the gods. Getting one up also showed the pharaoh's power and the organization of Egyptian society. Thousands of workers, skilled builders and farmers among them, had to cut the huge stones, move them, and set them in place. The Great Pyramid of Giza, built for Pharaoh Khufu, is about 4,500 years old. It was the tallest human made structure for thousands of years. They were royal tombs, but they kept on as a lasting sign of the Egyptian religion, the engineering, the teamwork, and the respect for their rulers' legacy.

Jay Gatsby is a tragic hero in the old sense. He has a great reach and a great blind spot. The blind spot is that he keeps an old dream for a living and mistakes it for the world he is in. He has made his fortune out of criminal activity, and the Daisy he keeps in his head is only partly the real woman. That does not make him less great. It makes the end more painful. You can see the whole thing in the green light across the water. It looks close enough to get. The water will not let him get it. The innocent girl he remembers is gone, and the old time he wants is gone with her. He will not take that in. For him money, hard work, and enough faith can put the lost time back. The moment he tells Nick that he can repeat the past shows how much the dream has him. The trouble is not that he loves Daisy. It is that he has made an ideal of her.

The end comes in Chapter 8. Daisy is the one who drives the car that kills Myrtle. Gatsby goes out to take the blame and stays there. Daisy does not speak. Wilson, in grief and wanting payback, comes to the pool and shoots him. Nobody is there for Gatsby when he dies. He goes out of the world with that dream still in his hands. Daisy gets out of the responsibility. That is what makes the death tragic. He has given himself up for a person who will give nothing in return.

He has the two things a traditional tragic hero needs. The aspiration is what lifts him, and the fatal weakness is his inability to see the world as it is. The green light at the close of the story is not a sign that such dreams will be answered. It is the sign of a man going on and on after something he cannot reach. His hope was worth admiring. It also finished him.

Causes and Duration of the Cuban Missile Crisis

It all goes back to the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union during the Cold War. Fidel Castro got into power in Cuba in 1959 and set up a communist government. He also got close to the Soviet Union. That put the United States on edge, since it now had communism dangerously close to its territory. The April 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion made that fear worse. American-supported Cuban exiles went in to try to overthrow Castro and failed. The failure made Castro stronger and left him sure the United States might try to invade again.

Nikita Khrushchev had his own reasons. Putting nuclear missiles in Cuba would protect Castro, push Soviet influence into the Western Hemisphere, and improve the Soviet Union's strategic position. The United States already kept nuclear missiles in Turkey and Italy, close to Soviet territory. That sort of move from the other side could make for a balance of power and show that the Soviet Union would not be intimidated by America.

The crisis ran for thirteen days, from 16 to 28 October 1962. Both sides were under enormous pressure and both wanted to keep from getting into a nuclear war. American surveillance planes found the missile sites. President Kennedy then had to pick a course that would not make him look weak and yet would not provoke an attack. He did not bomb Cuba at once. He ordered a naval "quarantine" to stop further Soviet shipments, and at the same time he secretly considered military action. That bought time for diplomacy, though it let the tension keep building.

It kept getting longer through misunderstandings, delays in communication, and the trouble of keeping military forces in check. A U.S. invasion might have brought Soviet retaliation. Soviet commanders in Cuba had nuclear weapons that American leaders did not know about. In the end Khrushchev agreed to take the missiles away. The price was a public American promise not to invade Cuba and a secret agreement to remove U.S. missiles from Turkey. Kennedy's caution and the private negotiations let the two men get to that compromise, and so the crisis ended before it could become a nuclear war.

The point was to find out whether the mass of a pendulum affects its period. The 50 g and 200 g bobs both gave a period of about 1.4 seconds on the same 0.5 m string. That period is the time for one complete back and forth swing. Inside the limits of the experiment, changing the mass did not significantly change it. The pendulum equation, \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}\), says the same. It makes the period depend mainly on the length of the string and the acceleration due to gravity, not on the mass of the bob. For a 0.5 m pendulum the expected period comes out to about 1.42 seconds, and the measured 1.4 seconds is very close. The results support the scientific theory.

The stopwatch was the first trouble. Starting and stopping it by hand puts reaction time into the figure. Air resistance, friction at the support, and slightly different release angles worked in the same way. If the angle got too large the period would not have matched the ideal equation as closely. Measuring only one or a few swings made the results less reliable.

Timing 10 or 20 swings and dividing the total time by the number of swings would have helped. Repeating each measurement several times and calculating an average would have helped more. Taken together the experiment showed that the pendulum's mass had little or no effect on its period when the string length remained constant.

This is how photosynthesis lets green plants get their food. The word equation for the whole thing is:

carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen

You still need light and chlorophyll to get it off the ground. The light gets caught by the chlorophyll in the chloroplasts. Those are the tiny structures inside the plant cells. The process mostly goes on in the leaves. The chlorophyll is a green pigment, and it is what takes in the light energy from the Sun.

The plant is also taking in carbon dioxide from the air through the stomata, the small openings in the leaves. The roots get water out of the soil. That water gets carried up the stem to the leaves in special tubes. Once the light energy is available, the plant puts the carbon dioxide and water to work in a series of chemical reactions. The result is glucose and oxygen.

Glucose is a sugar and it is what the plant mostly lives on. Some of it gets used right away in respiration to get the energy needed for growth and the rest of the plant's life processes. The extra gets turned into starch and put away in the roots, stems, fruits, or seeds. The plant also makes cellulose from it to strengthen the cell walls. It puts glucose to work in making other things needed for healthy growth.

The oxygen that comes out is a waste product. It gets let off into the atmosphere through the stomata. That does not make it less necessary, since humans and animals have to have it for respiration. You might as well say the whole business is what keeps almost all living organisms from going under. It gets food out, gets oxygen out, and takes the carbon dioxide out of the air. That same process helps the plants get on. It is what a lot of the food chains in the world get started from. Most of the life on Earth would run out of both food and oxygen if it ever stopped.

You get the whole thing from a 23.5 degree lean in the axis. That lean keeps looking the same way out in space while the planet goes around. The sun ends up hitting the ground at different angles because of it. The northern side gets the most direct of it in one stretch. That brings the long days and the warm weather. The southern side is pointed the other way at that time and gets the short cold days. You are looking at the whole thing from the other side six months out. The southern side gets the long days and the warmth then. The northern side has to go through its own cold stretch. The two in between happen when the tilt is not aimed at the sun. Getting a bit closer to the sun during the trip has nothing to do with it. The slant of the light and the length of the day are the only things that matter. That whole setup is what keeps the thing going.

The whole thing is water in constant motion through the Earth's atmosphere and surface. The Sun heats the water in the oceans, lakes, rivers, and the puddles. That liquid comes back up as invisible vapor. Higher in the sky it is cooler, so the vapor gives up heat. It then settles into tiny droplets on bits of dust, and that is how you get clouds. Once the clouds get heavy with those droplets or ice crystals, the water comes down as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. From there the water gets back to the Earth's surface and settles into the oceans, lakes, rivers, glaciers, and underground. Plants take some in, and animals drink the water. The Sun warms that collected water and the whole thing starts over. It supplies fresh water for living things, wears the land into new shapes, and keeps the Earth's temperature from getting out of hand. Without the water cycle life on this planet would not last very long at all.

Before the press, books got copied by hand, and often the copyists were monks. That made them expensive and rare. Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing press around 1440. It used movable metal type, ink, and a press. Printers could get many identical pages out in a hurry. Europe got written information faster, cheaper, and easier to share. A book market sprang up, and more people learned to read.

With more books around, ideas crossed borders and social classes. Scholars could set one text beside another and build on one another's discoveries. The press carried works on art, science, history, and Greece and Rome, which helped the Renaissance along. It also let scientists such as Copernicus and Vesalius share observations. Better maps and manuals did the same for trade, navigation, and education.

Religion and politics got the same treatment. Martin Luther put his criticisms of the Catholic Church into pamphlets, and that helped start the Protestant Reformation. Governments and churches got a wider way to push laws and beliefs. So did people who wanted to spread propaganda, rumors, and hatred. As literacy increased, people began to question traditional authorities and take part in debates.

The changes did not reach everyone equally. Women, poor people, and those living in rural areas often had less access to schooling and books. Printers sometimes faced censorship when rulers feared rebellion or criticism. The press still changed society permanently. It made the exchange of knowledge quicker, strengthened education and religious change, and helped develop modern science, politics, and culture. Its greatest effect was giving ideas a larger audience.

You got 18 mL of CO₂ out of the yeast in 20 minutes at 35°C. At 15°C it only got 6 mL out. That works out to 0.9 mL per minute against 0.3, so the whole thing ran three times as fast on the hot side. The yeast is just breaking down glucose for energy. Without much oxygen it goes through fermentation to get there, which leaves you with ethanol and the carbon dioxide you measured. The whole thing runs on enzymes. You warm the mix up from 15 to 35 and the enzyme and substrate particles end up with more kinetic energy. They get around faster and hit each other more often, and more of those hits end up being successful. That is why you see so much more gas. You get the opposite at 15, where the particles are too slow to get much done. That does not mean you could keep pushing the temperature and keep getting more out of it. Get past the yeast's own limit and the enzymes start to lose their shape and stop working. You might have hit that limit right around 35, but you would have to try more temperatures to be sure.

The whole thing was also at the mercy of the glucose concentration, how much yeast you used, the pH, and how well the gas measuring gear was set up. You would have to run it again and again at each temperature to get a mean you could trust. That means keeping the same apparatus, volumes, yeast concentration, and time period for every single one. A water bath would take care of the temperature side of things, and a quick check for leaks would keep the gas figures from getting mixed up. That much you can say for sure from what you got.

Five days in a row of early wake up times wears students out. You get a lot out of a four day week. The three day weekend gives time to rest, get homework done, and get out and do other things. Kids walk back in on Monday with more to give. Teachers get some of that same breathing room to plan and grade. That keeps them from burning out, and it shows in the classes they put together. Families can get to appointments and just be together without the whole thing falling through the cracks.

You will hear that this means longer days or less actual learning. You can get around that by stretching the day or keeping the fifth one for optional tutoring, clubs, and meals. That fifth day also has to cover childcare for the families that need it. You get less stress and better concentration out of the deal. That is a lot for a change that is this easy to put in place.

You get enough electricity from twelve turbines to run about 9,000 homes. That gets you off coal, oil, and gas. You also stop the carbon dioxide that comes with that kind of power. The air gets cleaner, which helps the children and older people in town. The wind does not run out the way fossil fuels do. That keeps your energy supply from getting caught up in rising fuel prices.

The money side of the thing works out too. You get a batch of jobs during the construction phase. The town ends up with extra tax money to put toward the schools, the roads, and the parks. You still need people around to keep the machines in shape after that. A place like this can draw in visitors who want to see how renewable energy works. The land around the turbines will still do for farming or grazing if you plan it right.

You will get complaints about the noise and the look of the thing. There is a chance of harm to the birds. You can put the machines far enough from the houses to cut down on the sound. Modern designs already do a lot to keep that down. You get the same protection for the wildlife by having experts watch over it. The town needs to set out those safety rules and leave a way for the people to get in a word before any of the work starts. That is all you need to get the thing moving.

For a $15 Federal Minimum Wage

You can't live on $7.25 an hour. That has been the federal floor since 2009. Work it full time and you end up with about $15,000 a year before taxes. That does not cover rent, food, getting around, or any kind of health care. After forty hours a week a lot of people are still in poverty or have to take public assistance. They should not have to.

You will hear that a $15 wage would force small businesses to raise prices, cut hours, or let people go. That risk is real, and it will be worse in places where living costs are already low. The other side is that better pay keeps people around. You get less quitting and more effort in return. You also stop paying over and over to hire and train. The money goes back into the local economy, since people with more of it buy more. That helps the community and lets workers keep a fairer share of what they put in.

One number for the whole country will not fit every town. You could roll the thing out by stages or let regional policies fill in the gaps. The point is to get a strong standard from the federal government. Nobody who works full time should be unable to get the basics.

The change will not fix every economic trouble. It is still an important step. People get more to spend and fewer get stuck in poverty. That makes for a stronger economy and a fairer one.

**How Social Media Affects Teenagers’ Sleep**

You get a lot out of social media. It carries messages, moves ideas around, and keeps people posted. The trouble starts when that happens after midnight. In our class, 19 out of 27 students are still on their phones then. That is a lot, and it may be getting into their health and their schoolwork.

You mean to look at one message. The next thing you know you have been watching videos, reading posts, and following comment threads for hours. The whole thing is made to hold your attention, and the clock gets lost. That costs sleep. The bright screen does the same, since the brain takes it as a sign to stay awake. It is worse right before bed. Notifications, messages, and online arguments will only wind you up. You end up too excited, worried, or stressed to get to sleep.

The payback comes the next day. It is harder to pay attention in class, to hold on to what has been said, and to get homework done. You are more likely to be irritable and to feel like doing nothing. Keep that up and it will get into your body and your head.

You can take some of the edge off. Pick a set time to quit for the night. Put the phone out of the bedroom, kill the pings, and get a regular alarm clock. Schools and families ought to be teaching students that too. The class figures show that this is not just a few people having trouble. If the night ends with the screens off, the sleep should come back and school will go better.

Our school got 1.2 tons of paper out of the trash last year. That kept a lot of it from taking up space in a landfill. The bins took in paper, cans, bottles, and cardboard. That helps, since the factories would not have to make as many new products from raw materials. Some of the trees, water, and energy that would have gone toward that work is saved. The pollution they put out goes down too. Getting that much done got students and teachers working together. The rest falls to the people who use the bins. Put the right things in the right one. Keep using a notebook instead of throwing it out. Skip the products that come wrapped in too much packaging. Recycling will not carry the whole load. Buying less and using things more than once have to go with it. That is how the daily choices add up to cleaner neighborhoods, healthier air, and a safer future. It also gets other people to do the same, which is as good a way as any to show some respect for the place we all live in. Kids are part of this. The choices made now are the ones future generations will have to live with.

The place smelled like old cardboard and a lot of different spices. I had six hours to fill and no idea of how the day would go. The people already there got me set up fast. It was mostly the same thing all the way through, checking dates on cans and getting them into boxes. You get used to the work. What you do not get used to is the amount of stuff that ends up there. Stores and people are dumping in far more than you would guess.

You have to keep your eyes on the labels and your voice down. The people coming in do not want to be made a show of. I got to see that up close when a parent took a full box of groceries off the line. The thanks kept coming in a way that made the whole morning seem to add up. I was too tired to think much of it on the way home. I have since told my friends they should get in on it. That is the only part of it that really seems to matter.

You get the result of a real infection without the sickness that would come with it. The body is shown a virus or bacterium in some altered form. That form might be a weakened or killed specimen. It might be a single protein, a bit of genetic instruction, or some other harmless part. All of these things are antigens. The immune cells take a look, mistake the thing for a live invader, and set about it. The attack they put together is more aimed and more effective with each try.

That attack depends heavily on the B cells. A share of them end up as plasma cells, and those plasma cells pump out antibodies. The antibodies are proteins that fasten to the pathogen's antigens. Once attached they can block the thing from getting in or they can tag it for destruction. Either result keeps the infection from taking hold or keeps the sickness from getting worse.

You get a second sort of B cell out of the business. These are the memory cells. They hang around after the vaccine has been used up. If the real thing ever shows up, they get to work faster and with more force. The system may also make some memory T cells. Those are the ones that keep the whole operation from getting out of hand or that go after the cells the germ has already gotten into.

It is that stored up experience that gets the germ stopped. A vaccinated person will often have it killed off before it gets to the point of causing disease. That is not always enough to keep the germ out. You can still get infected. What you are much less likely to get is the severe illness, the complications, or the chance of the thing getting around. To get that result you sometimes have to take more than one dose. The extra shots keep the protection from wearing off. That protection would otherwise thin out as the memory cells and antibodies run down.

The same thing works for the people you are mixed up with. A germ that cannot find a ready made host has a much harder time getting to the next. That stops it from reaching the people who cannot get the protection for themselves. You have had the system get that experience in a way that does not bring on the disease. The first time it meets an antigen it has in effect made the next meeting a thing it can deal with.

They are brave and helpful. They will go into a burning building to protect other people. When a fire gets going they get into the heavy clothing, the helmets, and the breathing gear and go in. The buildings are full of smoke. They get families and pets out, and sometimes they are saving people they have never met. You will find them at car accidents and in floods too. The work is exciting. It also takes training, teamwork, patience, and responsibility. I respect the way they keep a cool head and follow a careful plan while they are in so much danger. They get out to a neighborhood to show people how to check smoke alarms and make an escape plan. If I got the chance to meet one I would thank that person for the work and ask what it has been like. You do not need special powers to be a hero. Courage, kindness, and hard work will do. I want to do that much for my own community.

We lost 3-2 and I had to sit with that for a bit. We had run our opening arguments over and over so the score stung. My side put its weight behind the idea that solar and wind power cut down on pollution. We also tried to show that the technology is getting better and cheaper. The other team was ready with a list of problems including bad weather and the cost of storing power. They also brought up the damage that mining for battery materials does to the land. That whole approach to the topic had left me with almost no research into our own weaknesses.

I kept my head down trying to get my own lines out, which meant I missed out on some of the evidence they put forward. Writing things down and answering the question that was actually asked would have been a lot better. We also had some trouble getting from one speaker to the next and that made the whole thing sound less solid. The thing is that I am glad I was able to get through it with some confidence. You cannot look at the matter without seeing both the good and the bad. Getting more of a balance in the evidence is the first thing to work on. Letting the other side get in a word is the second. That sort of back and forth is what gets you to think things through.

You can tell a lot about a product from how it looks. You can t tell much about paper towels. They all look about the same so I set up a test to see which of three brands actually took in the most water. I figured the thickest and most expensive one would win out. That turned out to be wrong. The middle priced brand ended up absorbing the most.

The setup was pretty simple. I cut the three brands into the same sized pieces. I measured out the water and ran the whole thing three times for each one. That gave me enough to work with to get an average. You still have to watch for the things that could have thrown that off. It is hard to get the squeeze to be exactly the same every time. That is one of the reasons I would want to use a measuring device to keep the pressure the same. It would also be worth it to get in some more brands.

You get to 37 by starting with the 25 that is due every month. That first part of the bill does not change with usage. The rest of the amount has to come from the 0.10 that each text adds on. That gives you 25 + 0.10t = 37, with t standing in for the number of texts. Take the 25 away from both sides and you are left with 0.10t = 12. You are then just asking how many ten cent groups are in twelve dollars. The answer to 12 ÷ 0.10 is 120.

You can see that works by running the 120 back through the first equation. That many texts at 0.10 each makes 12. Put the 25 back in and you land right on the 37 that was on the bill. That makes 120 the number of texts sent. This only works because the bill you are looking at has no other fees or taxes in it.

Most places still make you wait until you are eighteen to get a ballot. That is a hold out from people who just assume sixteen year olds are not up to the task. Austria went ahead and cut that bar back in 2007. You can look at what has happened there since then. The kids in question are already paying the price for the rules that get made. They have to live with the choices that get handed down on their schools, their trains, and the state of the air they breathe. Putting a vote in their hands is likely to get them more interested in all that. They are going to have to put in some work to get that far. They are also going to have a say in the things that will end up shaping the rest of their lives.

You will hear that a lot of them simply do not have the knowledge or the maturity to get it right. Some will just take their cue from their parents, their friends, or the latest thing they see on a social media feed. That is a fair enough worry. The same goes for the fact that the whole thing demands a fair bit of understanding of taxes, the economy, and what is going on in the world. The idea that a person has to wait until they are more independent to get that understanding is where the whole thing gets stuck. The only way to get out of that is to have the schools start on the job. That means getting the kids to see how the elections actually work. They also have to learn to tell the reliable information from the rest of it.

You are not going to end up with a group of perfectly wise voters by making the change. That is just as true for the people who are already over the eighteen line. The move is still the right thing to do since it treats the interests of the young as something worth having. The schools have to get in there and supply the missing background. That is the only way the extra group of them is going to get much out of the process.

The buzzing happens in every classroom now. The phones do some good while they are there. They get a kid in touch with his parents, get an answer to a question, and now and then get an assignment organized. They will also get him into the games, videos, and social media that the devices carry. The notifications are not always meant to be rude. They still break a person's concentration, and once that has happened an important explanation is gone. The teacher has to stop and get the devices put away. That is time the class does not get back.

For most of the school day the phones should be kept off. You would get a quieter and fairer room to work in. The students would be more ready to take part in the work, to talk it over with one another, and to get out of a fix on their own. You would also see less of the old business of looking up answers or photographing a test. The whole place might get its attention back and learn to be more responsible for want of that constant outside help.

That does not mean the things have to be locked away forever. A kid who has to reach his family for medical reasons needs to be able to do so. Keeping the phones in a locker or a backpack and switching them off would cover that. The same goes for the approved emergencies the school has in mind. If a teacher wants to put the things to some particular educational use he can do so. One plainly stated set of rules will keep everyone from being treated in two different ways.

The school day is not going to get any better if the phones are left in charge. Keep them out of the lessons and the breaks and you will have a class that can pay attention and keep to its rules. You keep the kids safe that way and the work the teachers have approved still gets done.

*Of Mice and Men* gets under your skin. The Great Depression had people wandering from job to job, and it was easy to get left out. George and Lennie kept one off chance alive, the farm they meant to have. Lennie got into trouble over and over, not because he meant to, but because he had no idea what his own strength could do. That is what makes him a victim instead of a villain.

George had to do the worst thing he could, and it was the right thing. Lennie had accidentally killed Curley’s wife, and he was too scared to run. If the men found him they would have given him a cruel end. George shot him while he was still talking about that place. It was a mercy, and it still tore him apart. You are left wondering whether that kind of mercy can wear the face of violence. Two people can keep one another from going under. The cost can be too high to pay.

We wanted to know how much time a typical student puts into homework on a school night. Sixty of our grade took a short anonymous questionnaire to find out. Nobody had to take it and we collected no names. Everyone just gave a number for the minutes they usually work. We ran that list from the smallest amount of time to the largest and put it into a frequency table and a box-and-whisker plot.

That work paid off in the median of 75 minutes. With 60 responses that number is the average of the 30th and 31st values in the ordered list. It means half the group was done in that time or less and the rest took longer. You get a much better picture of the norm that way since a few students working for several hours would drag the mean around. The whole thing does point to homework eating up a good part of the evening. You can only trust that for the 60 volunteers we got and their own estimates of the time involved. Workload shifts by the day and the subject anyway. Getting more people to answer over several days would be the way to get a better look. We did end up putting data collection and measures of center to work on a real question.

I worked twenty hours a week at a grocery store this summer. The hours filled up with unloading deliveries, organizing products, checking expiration dates, cleaning aisles, and helping customers find what they needed. The work got to be a lot of the same thing. You learn pretty fast that consistency matters. A misplaced item or an empty shelf made shopping rough for the next person and gave your coworkers extra to do.

Weekends were the worst. Lines got long fast and people got testy. I had to keep my voice even, work faster, and ask for help when the job got ahead of me. The first few times I worked the register I kept expecting to mess up. That worry wore off. You get used to taking payments, answering questions, and straightening out the smaller snags. Being friendly was only part of the job. You had to listen and answer people in a way that kept things moving.

No one on the crew could get through a shift alone. We all had our own set of duties, and when one of us got behind the rest of us picked up the slack. That made the harder stretches easier to get through. My manager also pointed out what I was doing well and where I needed to get better.

Getting my own money made me watch where it went a lot more closely. Showing up on a regular schedule made the idea of commitment something I could actually see. The job wore me out on more than one occasion. It also gave me some of the ground to stand on when I have to take on more later on. You can get a lot out of an ordinary job if you go at it with a positive attitude.

The day I broke my wrist I was sure missing basketball season would be the worst of it. The cast got on and I found out I cared more about not being able to play guitar. I had taught myself for two years, and that was the place I went when things got too much. Chords and strumming were out with the wrist pinned. I kept saying a few months away would be no big deal. It did not help. The thing in the corner of the room kept showing me what I had lost, and the whole thing grew bigger than the injury.

My physical therapist got me to look at progress instead of perfection. I listened to songs and went over chord diagrams. Once the doctor gave the okay for movement, I worked on one finger at a time. I took songs down to a simpler form, shifted my hand, and got a different hold on the pick. Ten minutes usually got me only a little way, but it got me there. There was no big scene of it. I just kept trying when the wrist hurt and the playing came out clumsy. I did get through a whole song for my family. It was plain, and getting to the end mattered because I had rebuilt both the confidence and the strength.

That broken wrist showed that resilience is mostly adapting, not getting back to the way things were. I do the same with schoolwork and the other setbacks that pile up. I break them into steps I can handle, get some help, and measure progress patiently. The guitar is still there, and I have picked up a different way of going about it. The limits may change the method, but they do not decide the end.

You can see it in a right triangle with legs of 3 and 4 units. The side opposite the right angle, the hypotenuse, comes out to 5. Put a square on the 3 unit side and you get an area of 9 square units. Do the same for the 4 unit side and the area is 16. Those two add up to 25, which is exactly the area of the square you get on the 5 unit side. That 9 + 16 = 25 result isn't a fluke. Take four such triangles and fit them inside a larger square. You can do it in two different ways and the four triangles always take up the same amount of room. The space left over in one case is a single square on the hypotenuse, while in the other it is the two squares on the legs. They have to be the same size. That is the rule a² + b² = c², where a and b are the legs and c is the hypotenuse. It works for every right triangle.

For a circle you want A = πr². A is the area and r the radius, the distance from the center out to the edge. Pi is a number you can take as 3.14. With a radius of 4 centimeters you put 4 in for r and get A = π × 4². The 4 squared is 16, so A is 16π square centimeters. That 16 times 3.14 gives 50.24, so the circle has an area of about 50.24 square centimeters. The ratio between the circumference and the diameter is the same for every circle, and that ratio is what pi is. It keeps that value whether the circle is large or small. The formula comes from the fact that you can cut a circle into many thin slices and put the slices together to make something close to a rectangle. That rectangle will have one side about the radius and the other about half the circumference.

The conch is the most important symbol in Lord of the Flies because it stands for the rules the boys try to keep. At first it is only a pretty shell that Ralph and Piggy use to gather everyone together. That first use gives the boys a reason to talk and to make laws. As long as the shell is honored, the group keeps something like a civilized order. Any boy who holds it has the right to speak, and that simple idea keeps the worst of their natures in check. The shell therefore becomes the only thing that can replace the grown up world they have lost. It also reminds the group that they once had a common purpose beyond hunting and fear. Whenever the shell is brought out, the boys are forced to face that earlier agreement. Its sound can be heard across the island, and this makes the object seem like a voice. That voice is only one the boys have chosen to accept.

This order does not depend on the shell itself. It depends on the boys' willingness to believe that it has power. When Jack begins to ignore the rules, he is really attacking that shared belief. The final destruction of the shell shows that the last defense against savagery has been thrown away. From that point on there is no common authority to call the group back to reason. Golding uses the object to show that civilization is far more fragile than it appears.

My first time on the school stage happened last spring. I had to read a poem for the whole class. In the weeks before it, I had practiced in front of a mirror, and my mother had listened to me many times. That did not stop my stomach from twisting when the final day arrived.

I had tried to talk myself out of the performance, but the more I did that, the worse the fear got. It felt as if the whole audience were watching my every move from then. The room was full of faces I knew. Some of them were smiling, while others seemed to be waiting to see if I would fail. When my name was called, my legs felt as though they had turned to lead. I walked to the front, and the bright lights made everything else fade away.

For the first few lines, my voice was little more than a thin, shaky thing. Then I began to remember the words I had chosen. Before I knew it, the poem had become something that belonged to me. When I reached the end, the sudden burst of clapping seemed almost too much to take in.

Brian Robeson is thirteen when the pilot dies of a heart attack on the way to see his father. The plane crashes into a lake, and he is thrown into the water. He clings to a birch tree until the wreck breaks apart, then swims to a sandbar. With only a hatchet, a knife, and some torn clothes, he makes his way to the mainland. There he finds a shallow cave that gives him a little shelter. His first great task is to get a fire going, and he finally succeeds by striking the hatchet against flint. Once the flames are up, he tries to use them to send a signal to the outside world. That attempt brings him to the shore, where he notices a school of fish and decides to try to catch some for food. He has no idea what the coming days will bring for him.

Dear Editor,

You should keep the salad bar. Last week 140 of us used it, and that is a lot for a single week. If the number had been so small, it would have been easy to cut. Instead the bar has become one of the most popular parts of the lunch period. Many students use it to get some vegetables they would not otherwise eat. For some of us the bar is the only way to get a meal that fits our own needs.

The change would also hurt the whole group. Students who are trying to eat in a better way would be left with very few choices. That is not the kind of school we want. The bar has already been tried out and has worked. There is no reason to take it away now. The 140 students who got something from it are a clear sign that it belongs in the cafeteria.

If you are going to judge a part of the lunch period, you should look at the facts. Those facts show that the salad bar is both needed and wanted. Keeping it will do more good than cutting it ever could.

Sincerely,
A Student
